questions.title: Write a parameterized synchronous FIFO. How do you detect full and empty?
questions.answer:
Use pointers one bit wider than the address. Equal pointers = empty; only the MSB (wrap bit) differs = full.
Follow-ups: non-power-of-2 depth → wrap by hand at D-1 and keep an occupancy counter (full = count == D).
Read+write together when full: this design blocks the write; some specs allow it, check which one.
The memory has no reset: saves area, and the empty flag already hides stale data.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** make each pointer one bit wider than the address. The low bits index the RAM; the extra MSB is a *wrap bit* that flips each time the pointer laps the buffer. Equal pointers mean **empty**; same index but different wrap bit means the writer is exactly one lap ahead, i.e. **full**.

Trace for `D = 4` (AW = 2, pointers are 3 bits):

| Event | wptr | rptr | empty | full |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| reset | 000 | 000 | 1 | 0 |
| 4 writes | 100 | 000 | 0 | 1 (index 00 = 00, MSB differs) |
| 1 read | 100 | 001 | 0 | 0 |
| 3 reads | 100 | 100 | 1 | 0 |
| 4 writes | 000 (wrapped) | 100 | 0 | 1 |

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",   "wave": "p......." },
  { "name": "wr_en", "wave": "01.0...." },
  { "name": "wdata", "wave": "x==x....", "data": ["A", "B"] },
  { "name": "rd_en", "wave": "0...1.0." },
  { "name": "rdata", "wave": "x....==.", "data": ["A", "B"] },
  { "name": "empty", "wave": "1.0...1." }
],
  "head": { "text": "registered read: rdata is valid one cycle after rd_en" } }
```

### Solution
- `do_wr = wr_en && !full`, `do_rd = rd_en && !empty`: never move a pointer on an illegal access, so overflow and underflow are impossible by construction.
- Pointers have an async reset; the storage array and `rdata` have none (keeps reset out of the data path).
- Occupancy, if needed, is simply `wptr - rptr` in AW+1 bits.

### Code
```systemverilog
module sync_fifo #(parameter int W = 8, D = 16, localparam int AW = $clog2(D)) (
  input  logic         clk, rst_n, wr_en, rd_en,
  input  logic [W-1:0] wdata,
  output logic [W-1:0] rdata,
  output logic         full, empty
);
  logic [W-1:0] mem [D];
  logic [AW:0]  wptr, rptr;                  // extra MSB = wrap bit
  logic         do_wr, do_rd;

  assign empty = (wptr == rptr);
  assign full  = (wptr[AW] != rptr[AW]) && (wptr[AW-1:0] == rptr[AW-1:0]);
  assign do_wr = wr_en && !full;
  assign do_rd = rd_en && !empty;

  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)  // pointers: async reset
    if (!rst_n) begin
      wptr <= '0; rptr <= '0;
    end else begin
      if (do_wr) wptr <= wptr + 1'b1;
      if (do_rd) rptr <= rptr + 1'b1;
    end

  always_ff @(posedge clk) begin             // storage: no reset
    if (do_wr) mem[wptr[AW-1:0]] <= wdata;
    if (do_rd) rdata <= mem[rptr[AW-1:0]];   // valid 1 cycle after rd_en
  end
endmodule
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- The wrap-bit trick needs `D` to be a power of 2 (and at least 2). For other depths, wrap each pointer at `D-1` by hand and keep a counter: `full = (count == D)`.
- **Read and write in the same cycle while full:** this design rejects the write. Some specs allow it, since a slot frees up that cycle (`do_wr = wr_en && (!full || rd_en)`). Check which one the spec wants.
- While empty, a simultaneous read is rejected: there is no fall-through. A first-word-fall-through (FWFT) FIFO needs extra output logic.

### Follow-ups
- *almost_full / almost_empty?* Compare `wptr - rptr` with a threshold, and register it if timing is tight.
- *Why no reset on the memory?* It saves area and reset routing. The empty flag already stops anyone from reading stale data.
- *How would you verify it?* Use a queue reference model and SVA on the flags (see "How would you verify a FIFO?").

questions.title: Draw an async FIFO. Why use Gray-code pointers, and how are full and empty generated?
questions.answer:
Gray code changes one bit per increment, so a synchronizer sampling mid-transition gets the old or the new pointer, never a wrong one.
Write pointer (Gray) → 2 flops → read domain, where empty is computed. Read pointer (Gray) → 2 flops → write domain, where full is computed.
Empty: read Gray == synchronized write Gray. Full: top two bits inverted, rest equal.
Flags are pessimistic: they assert on time and deassert 2-3 cycles late, which is safe. Data needs no synchronizer: it is stable before the pointer says it is written.
Depth must be a power of 2. Constrain the Gray bus with set_max_delay -datapath_only / set_bus_skew. Know binary↔Gray conversions.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** each side keeps its own pointer and only sees a *synchronized, slightly stale* copy of the other side's pointer. Pointers cross as **Gray code**: only one bit changes per increment, so a 2-FF synchronizer that samples mid-change sees either the old or the new value, never a value the pointer never held.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph WD["write domain (wclk)"]
    WP["wbin / wgray"] --> FULL["full logic"]
    WS["wq2_rgray (2-FF sync)"] --> FULL
  end
  subgraph RAMB["dual-port RAM"]
    RAM["mem (2^AW entries)"]
  end
  subgraph RDOM["read domain (rclk)"]
    RP["rbin / rgray"] --> EMPTY["empty logic"]
    RS["rq2_wgray (2-FF sync)"] --> EMPTY
  end
  WP -->|waddr| RAM
  RP -->|raddr| RAM
  WP -->|wgray| RS
  RP -->|rgray| WS
```

Gray pointers for D = 4 (3-bit pointers, extra wrap bit):

| binary | 000 | 001 | 010 | 011 | 100 | 101 | 110 | 111 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gray | 000 | 001 | 011 | 010 | 110 | 111 | 101 | 100 |

After 4 writes and no reads, wgray = `110` and rgray = `000`. Invert the top two bits of rgray to get `110`, which equals wgray, so the FIFO is **full**. One lap apart in binary (MSB differs) shows up in Gray as *both* top bits differing.

### Explanation
- **Empty** (read domain): `rgray_next == rq2_wgray`.
- **Full** (write domain): `wgray_next == {~wq2_rgray[AW:AW-1], wq2_rgray[AW-2:0]}`.
- Both flags are registered from the *next* pointer values, so they update in the same cycle as the pointer.

### Code
```systemverilog
module async_fifo #(parameter int W = 8, AW = 4) (    // depth = 2**AW, AW >= 2
  input  logic         wclk, wrst_n, winc,
  input  logic [W-1:0] wdata,
  output logic         wfull,
  input  logic         rclk, rrst_n, rinc,
  output logic [W-1:0] rdata,
  output logic         rempty
);
  logic [W-1:0] mem [2**AW];
  logic [AW:0]  wbin, wgray, rbin, rgray, wbin_next, wgray_next, rbin_next, rgray_next;
  logic [AW:0]  wq1_rgray, wq2_rgray, rq1_wgray, rq2_wgray;

  // ---------------- write domain
  assign wbin_next  = wbin + (winc & ~wfull);
  assign wgray_next = (wbin_next >> 1) ^ wbin_next;
  always_ff @(posedge wclk or negedge wrst_n)
    if (!wrst_n) begin
      wbin <= '0; wgray <= '0; wfull <= 1'b0;
    end else begin
      wbin  <= wbin_next;
      wgray <= wgray_next;
      wfull <= (wgray_next == {~wq2_rgray[AW:AW-1], wq2_rgray[AW-2:0]});
    end
  always_ff @(posedge wclk)
    if (winc && !wfull) mem[wbin[AW-1:0]] <= wdata;
  always_ff @(posedge wclk or negedge wrst_n)          // rgray -> wclk domain
    if (!wrst_n) {wq2_rgray, wq1_rgray} <= '0;
    else         {wq2_rgray, wq1_rgray} <= {wq1_rgray, rgray};

  // ---------------- read domain
  assign rbin_next  = rbin + (rinc & ~rempty);
  assign rgray_next = (rbin_next >> 1) ^ rbin_next;
  always_ff @(posedge rclk or negedge rrst_n)
    if (!rrst_n) begin
      rbin <= '0; rgray <= '0; rempty <= 1'b1;
    end else begin
      rbin   <= rbin_next;
      rgray  <= rgray_next;
      rempty <= (rgray_next == rq2_wgray);
    end
  assign rdata = mem[rbin[AW-1:0]];                    // first-word fall-through read
  always_ff @(posedge rclk or negedge rrst_n)          // wgray -> rclk domain
    if (!rrst_n) {rq2_wgray, rq1_wgray} <= '0;
    else         {rq2_wgray, rq1_wgray} <= {rq1_wgray, wgray};
endmodule
```

Conversions you should be able to write on the spot:
```systemverilog
assign g_out = b_in ^ (b_in >> 1);                     // binary -> Gray
always_comb begin                                      // Gray -> binary
  b_out[N-1] = g_in[N-1];
  for (int i = N-2; i >= 0; i--) b_out[i] = b_out[i+1] ^ g_in[i];
end
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- **Flags are pessimistic, and that is safe.** Each flag *asserts* on time, because the pointer that causes it is local. It *deasserts* 2–3 cycles late, because the other pointer is stale. The FIFO can't overflow or underflow, but it gets a little less throughput, so add a few entries of depth.
- **No synchronizer on the data:** the reader only reads an entry after the synchronized pointer says it was written, and by then the data has been stable for 2 or more cycles.
- **Depth must be a power of 2,** or the Gray sequence is no longer one-bit-change at the wrap. Other depths need a special Gray sequence.
- **Timing constraint:** add `set_max_delay -datapath_only` or `set_bus_skew` on the Gray bus, so the skew between its bits stays under one source clock period. Otherwise two bits could change in the same sampling window.

### Follow-ups
- *Why not synchronize a binary pointer?* 0111→1000 flips 4 bits. If they resolve on different cycles, the receiver could see 1111, a false pointer far ahead.
- *How do you verify it?* Sweep the clock ratios (fast/slow/equal), reset each domain on its own, add an SVA that the Gray pointer changes by `$onehot0` per cycle, and run formal CDC.

questions.title: How does a 2-FF synchronizer work? Why can't you use it for a multi-bit bus?
questions.answer:
The first flop may go metastable; it gets a full clock cycle to settle before the second flop samples it. MTBF = e^(tr/tau) / (T0 * fclk * fdata); a third flop multiplies MTBF by about e^(T/tau).
Multi-bit bus: each bit may resolve on a different cycle, so the receiver can see a value that never existed.
Fixes: Gray code (counters stepping ±1), req/ack handshake or async FIFO, mux recirculation with a synchronized enable.
Fast-to-slow pulse: stretch it, or convert to a toggle and edge-detect after syncing.
Same frequency, different phase: one PLL with a fixed known offset is STA-timed (synchronous); unknown or drifting phase is a CDC.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** the first flop may sample a changing input and go **metastable**. It gets almost one full destination clock period to resolve before the second flop samples it, so the probability that metastability reaches the logic drops exponentially. It works per *bit*, so a bus whose bits resolve on different cycles can show a value that never existed.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk_dst",       "wave": "p......." },
  { "name": "d (async)",     "wave": "0.1....." },
  { "name": "q1",            "wave": "0..x1..." },
  { "name": "q2 (to logic)", "wave": "0...1..." },
  {},
  { "name": "bus src",       "wave": "=..=....", "data": ["01", "10"] },
  { "name": "bus after sync","wave": "=...==..", "data": ["01", "11", "10"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "q1 may go metastable but settles within a cycle; bus bits settle on different cycles and show 11" } }
```

### Explanation
- `MTBF = e^(t_r / tau) / (T0 * f_clk * f_data)`. Here `t_r` is the resolution time (about one clock period minus setup), `tau` and `T0` are flop constants, and `f_clk` and `f_data` are the clock and data-toggle rates. A third flop adds another period of `t_r`, which multiplies MTBF by about `e^(T/tau)`. Use it at very high clock rates.
- **Multi-bit bus:** each bit has its own synchronizer and its own chance of resolving one cycle late, so `01 → 10` can be seen as `11` or `00` for a cycle.

| Multi-bit scheme | Use when |
| --- | --- |
| Gray code + 2-FF per bit | counters that step by ±1 (FIFO pointers) |
| req/ack handshake | occasional control or config words |
| async FIFO | streaming data |
| mux recirculation (sync only an enable) | data held stable while a 1-bit `load` crosses |

### Code
Fast-to-slow single pulse: convert it to a toggle, synchronize the toggle, then edge-detect.
```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk_s or negedge rst_s_n)        // source: pulse -> level toggle
  if (!rst_s_n)     tgl <= 1'b0;
  else if (pulse_s) tgl <= ~tgl;

always_ff @(posedge clk_d or negedge rst_d_n)        // destination: 2-FF sync + 1 history
  if (!rst_d_n) {s3, s2, s1} <= '0;
  else          {s3, s2, s1} <= {s2, s1, tgl};
assign pulse_d = s3 ^ s2;                            // one dst-cycle pulse per source pulse
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- No combinational logic in front of the first flop. Glitches multiply the effective `f_data`, and CDC tools flag it.
- A short pulse from a fast domain can fall between two slow clock edges and be missed. Stretch it, or use the toggle scheme above. Pulses closer together than about 2 destination cycles still merge.
- **Same frequency, different phase:** if both clocks come from one PLL with a fixed, known offset, STA can time the path. It is synchronous, just with a tight window. If the sources differ, or the phase is unknown or drifts, timing can't be closed, so treat it as a CDC.

### Follow-ups
- *Why not just add more flops to a bus?* More flops lower each bit's metastability risk, but the bits can still land on different cycles. Skew is the problem, not MTBF.
- *Can simulation show this?* No. RTL flops always resolve at once. Use CDC tools, or inject random one-cycle delays on synchronizer outputs.

questions.title: Calculate the minimum FIFO depth (e.g. write at 80 MHz, read at 50 MHz, 120-word burst).
questions.answer:
Example: write 80 MHz, read 50 MHz, 120-word burst, no idle cycles.
Time to write the burst = 120 / 80 MHz = 1500 ns. Words read in that time = 1500 ns × 50 MHz = 75. Depth = 120 − 75 = 45.
General: Depth = B − B·(f_rd·r_rd)/(f_wr·r_wr), r = fraction of active cycles.
Trap: "80 writes in any 100 cycles" → worst case is two windows back to back, so B = 160.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** the FIFO must absorb whatever the writer puts in faster than the reader takes out, over the *worst-case burst*. Depth = words written during the burst − words read during the same time.

Worked example: write at 80 MHz, read at 50 MHz, 120-word burst, no idle cycles on either side.

| Step | Calculation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Time to write the burst | 120 / 80 MHz | 1500 ns |
| Words read meanwhile | 1500 ns × 50 MHz | 75 |
| Minimum depth | 120 − 75 | **45** (implement 64 if it must be a power of 2) |

General formula, where `r` is the fraction of cycles that are active (idle cycles, duty cycle):
```text
Depth = B - B * (f_rd * r_rd) / (f_wr * r_wr)
```

### Explanation
- Only the **burst** matters. Over the long run the average write rate must be at or below the read rate, or no finite FIFO works.
- If the reader only reads every other cycle, `r_rd = 0.5`: 1500 ns × 25 MHz = 37.5, so 37 words are read and depth = 120 − 37 = **83**. Round in the pessimistic direction.

### The "X writes in any Y cycles" trap

| Spec | Worst case |
| --- | --- |
| "80 writes in any 100 write cycles" | 80 at the *end* of one window + 80 at the *start* of the next = **160 back-to-back writes** |

With 80 MHz write, 50 MHz read and continuous reads: 160 / 80 MHz = 2000 ns → 100 words read → depth = 160 − 100 = **60**.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Async FIFO: add a few entries for the 2–3 cycles of synchronizer latency on the flags, plus any read-side pipeline latency before the reader reacts.
- If reads start late (the reader needs N cycles after `!empty` to begin), add the words written in those N cycles.
- Check whether the burst sizes are in words or bytes, and whether the bus widths differ on the two sides.

### Follow-ups
- *Write slower than read?* Depth 1 (or 2 for timing) is enough for rate matching. The FIFO only handles CDC.
- *How do you check it in verification?* Cover max occupancy and full, and stress with the worst-case burst and the slowest reader.

questions.title: Design an overlapping 1101 sequence detector (Mealy). Then make it Moore.
questions.answer:
Each state = longest prefix of 1101 seen so far. After a detection the trailing 1 is itself a prefix, so go to S1, not S0.
Moore: add S4 = "1101 seen" with det = 1; from S4, 1 → S2 (suffix 11), 0 → S0. Output one cycle later than Mealy but glitch-free.
Non-overlapping: S3 on 1 → S0. Verify with a shift-register reference model: det_exp = (sr[3:0] == 4'b1101).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** each state remembers the **longest prefix of `1101`** that is also a suffix of the input so far. On a match, the last `1` is already a valid prefix, so the overlapping detector goes to **S1**, not S0.

Mealy (output on the transition, `in/out`):
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> S0
  S0 --> S1: 1/0
  S0 --> S0: 0/0
  S1 --> S2: 1/0
  S1 --> S0: 0/0
  S2 --> S2: 1/0
  S2 --> S3: 0/0
  S3 --> S1: 1/1
  S3 --> S0: 0/0
```

Trace for input `1101101` (overlapping):

| bit | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| state after | S1 | S2 | S3 | S1 | S2 | S3 | S1 |
| det (Mealy) | 0 | 0 | 0 | **1** | 0 | 0 | **1** |

### Code
```systemverilog
module det1101 (input logic clk, rst_n, din, output logic det);
  typedef enum logic [1:0] {S0, S1, S2, S3} st_t;
  st_t st, nst;
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) st <= S0;
    else        st <= nst;
  always_comb begin
    nst = st; det = 1'b0;                 // defaults prevent latches
    case (st)
      S0: nst = din ? S1 : S0;
      S1: nst = din ? S2 : S0;
      S2: nst = din ? S2 : S3;
      S3: begin nst = din ? S1 : S0; det = din; end
    endcase
  end
endmodule
```

Moore version (output depends on the state only):
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> S0
  S0 --> S1: 1
  S0 --> S0: 0
  S1 --> S2: 1
  S1 --> S0: 0
  S2 --> S2: 1
  S2 --> S3: 0
  S3 --> S4: 1
  S3 --> S0: 0
  S4 --> S2: 1
  S4 --> S0: 0
```
`S4` means "1101 seen" and drives `det = 1`. From S4, a `1` makes the suffix `11`, so go to S2. A `0` makes `11010`, and no suffix of that is a prefix of 1101, so go to S0.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- **Moore vs Mealy:** Moore adds a state, and `det` comes one cycle later, but it is glitch-free because it comes straight from state flops. Mealy reacts in the same cycle, but `det` follows `din` combinationally.
- **Non-overlapping:** in S3, input 1 goes to S0 instead of S1.
- S2 on `1` stays in S2 (`111` still ends with `11`). Sending it to S0 is the classic bug.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you verify it?* Use a shift-register reference model in the scoreboard, `det_exp = (sr[3:0] == 4'b1101)`, and drive random bits plus directed overlapping patterns (`1101101`, `111101`).
- *Encoding?* Binary uses 2 flops for 4 states. One-hot uses more flops but makes next-state logic simpler and faster.

questions.title: Write a rising-, falling- and any-edge detector. Generate a one-cycle pulse when req rises.
questions.answer:
Register the input once (d_q) and compare: rise = d & ~d_q, fall = ~d & d_q, any = d ^ d_q.
If d is asynchronous, synchronize it first (2 flops) and detect on the synchronized copy.
Hardware: one DFF plus an AND gate with an inverted input.

questions.title: Divide a clock by 3 with a 50% duty cycle.
questions.answer:
Make a 1/3-duty signal on the posedge, delay it by half a period with a negedge flop, and combine: high time becomes 1.5T out of 3T.
(The card's toggle version needs the second flop on the negedge, and its cnt declaration is missing a semicolon.)
Follow-ups: divide-by-2 is a toggle flop; even N toggles every N/2 cycles. Output clocks need create_generated_clock. Gate clocks with an ICG (latch + AND), not a plain AND.

questions.title: Design a 4-request round-robin arbiter. How do you make a 128-bit one fast?
questions.answer:
Mask off every requester at or below the last grant and pick the lowest set bit; if nothing is left, fall back to the unmasked requests.
gnt_m = mreq & (~mreq + 1); gnt_u = req & (~req + 1); gnt = |mreq ? gnt_m : gnt_u; mask <= ~((gnt << 1) - 1) on a grant.
|mreq asks "is anyone still requesting above the last winner?" Yes → continue the round; no → wrap to bit 0.
Fixed priority: req & -req. Highest-bit-first: reverse with {<<{req}}. 128 bits: ~req+1 is an O(N) carry chain → parallel-prefix OR (O(log N)) or a tree of 4-input arbiters.
Verify: no starvation (granted within N grants), one-hot grant, no grant without request.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** run two lowest-bit-first priority arbiters in parallel. One sees only the requests **above the last winner** (`req & mask`), the other sees all requests. If anyone is left above the pointer, grant from the masked set and continue the round. Otherwise wrap around to bit 0.

Trace with N = 4 and `req = 4'b1011` held (requester 2 idle):

| Cycle | mask | mreq = req & mask | \|mreq | gnt | next mask |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1111 | 1011 | 1 | 0001 | 1110 |
| 2 | 1110 | 1010 | 1 | 0010 | 1100 |
| 3 | 1100 | 1000 | 1 | 1000 | 0000 |
| 4 | 0000 | 0000 | 0 | 0001 (wrap) | 1110 |

### Code
```systemverilog
module rr_arb #(parameter int N = 4) (
  input  logic         clk, rst_n,
  input  logic [N-1:0] req,
  output logic [N-1:0] gnt
);
  logic [N-1:0] mask, mreq, gnt_m, gnt_u;
  assign mreq  = req & mask;
  assign gnt_m = mreq & (~mreq + 1'b1);       // isolate lowest set bit
  assign gnt_u = req  & (~req  + 1'b1);
  assign gnt   = (|mreq) ? gnt_m : gnt_u;     // continue the round, or wrap
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n)    mask <= '1;
    else if (|gnt) mask <= ~((gnt << 1) - 1'b1);  // keep bits strictly above the winner
endmodule
```
`mask` is really a pointer to the last winner, and it only updates on a grant, so it holds while idle. For the top bit (`gnt = 1000`), `gnt << 1` overflows to 0 and the mask becomes `0000`, which forces a wrap on the next cycle.

### Variants
- **Fixed priority (LSB first):** `gnt = req & (~req + 1)`, i.e. `req & -req`.
- **Fixed priority, MSB first:** reverse, isolate, reverse back:
```systemverilog
assign req_r = {<<{req}};
assign gnt_r = req_r & (~req_r + 1'b1);
assign gnt   = {<<{gnt_r}};
```
- **Locked/sticky:** hold the grant until the winner drops `req` (bus ownership for a whole burst).

### Making a 128-bit one fast
- `~req + 1` is a ripple carry chain, O(N) deep when built naively. Replace "find the lowest set bit" with a **parallel-prefix OR** (`pre[i] = |req[i-1:0]`, `gnt[i] = req[i] & ~pre[i]`), which is O(log N) deep, or with a **tree of 4-input arbiters** (local winners per group plus a group-level round robin).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Check the pointer update with N not a power of 2 and with the top bit winning.
- Don't update the mask when there is no grant, or fairness breaks after idle periods.

### Follow-ups (verification)
- `assert property (@(posedge clk) $onehot0(gnt));` and `(gnt & ~req) == 0` (no grant without a request).
- **Starvation:** every held request is granted within N grants: `req[i] |-> ##[0:N-1] gnt[i]` when requests are held.
- Coverage: cross of the request vector with the last winner, wrap-around, and all requesters active together.

questions.title: Blocking vs non-blocking assignments: trace the hardware each one infers.
questions.answer:
B <= A; C <= B; → 2 flops in series (shift register). B = A; C = B; (clocked) → both B and C are flops of A; C loses a cycle of delay.
A = en ? 1 : C; B = A; C = B; with blocking → all take the same new value: one sticky flop (x <= en | x); with <= → a 3-stage ring.
Rule: <= in sequential, = in always_comb. Mixing across blocks causes simulation races.
Swap without a temp: a <= b; b <= a; or XOR swap a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b (works because x ^ k ^ k = x).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** non-blocking (`<=`) samples every right-hand side first, then updates all left-hand sides together at the end of the time step, like real flops. Blocking (`=`) updates right away, so the next statement sees the **new** value and stages collapse.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph NB["B <= A; C <= B (non-blocking)"]
    A1["A"] --> FB1["FF B"] --> FC1["FF C"]
  end
  subgraph BL["B = A; C = B (blocking, clocked)"]
    A2["A"] --> FB2["FF B"]
    A2 --> FC2["FF C"]
  end
```

| Code in `always @(posedge clk)` | Hardware |
| --- | --- |
| `B <= A; C <= B;` | 2-stage shift register: C is A delayed 2 cycles |
| `B = A; C = B;` | B and C are both flops of A: C lost a stage |
| `A = en ? 1 : C; B = A; C = B;` | all three get the same new value: one sticky flop, `x <= en \| x` |
| same with `<=` | 3-stage ring: A ← en \| C, B ← A, C ← B |

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",            "wave": "p......" },
  { "name": "A",              "wave": "01.0..." },
  { "name": "C (non-blocking)", "wave": "0..1.0." },
  { "name": "C (blocking)",   "wave": "0.1.0.." }
],
  "head": { "text": "B <= A; C <= B gives 2 cycles of delay; B = A; C = B only gives 1" } }
```

### Explanation
- **Rule:** use `<=` in `always_ff` (sequential) and `=` in `always_comb`. Mixing them, or reading a blocking-assigned variable from another `always` block, creates simulation races whose result depends on the scheduler.
- Statement order matters with `=` (`C = B; B = A;` gives back a shift register). With `<=` order doesn't matter.

### XOR swap without a temporary
Relies on `x ^ x = 0`, `x ^ 0 = x`, and XOR being commutative, so `x ^ k ^ k = x`:

| step | a | b |
| --- | --- | --- |
| start | 1010 | 0110 |
| `a ^= b` | 1100 (A^B) | 0110 |
| `b ^= a` | 1100 | 1010 (= A) |
| `a ^= b` | 0110 (= B) | 1010 |

In hardware the simple answer is `a <= b; b <= a;` in one clocked block. Non-blocking makes it a true swap.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A blocking assignment to a variable that is read before it is written in the same clocked block still infers a flop (`C` in the third example).
- Don't use `#0` to "fix" races. Fix the coding style instead.

### Follow-ups
- *Which region does `<=` update in?* The NBA region, after all Active events of that time step.
- *Testbench driving DUT inputs at the clock edge?* Use a clocking block or `<=` so the DUT samples the old value.

questions.title: Define setup and hold time. How do you fix each violation, and which is harder to fix?
questions.answer:
Setup: T_clk ≥ t_c2q + t_logic,max + t_setup − t_skew. Hold: t_c2q + t_logic,min ≥ t_hold + t_skew. Skew = capture clock arrival − launch clock arrival.
Fix setup: pipeline, retime, upsize / low-Vt cells, reduce logic depth, lower the frequency as a last resort.
Fix hold: add delay buffers on the short path; frequency is not in the hold equation, so slowing the clock can't fix it.
Hold is worse: a setup violation still works at a lower clock, a hold violation fails at any frequency.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** **setup** = data must arrive and be stable *before* the capture edge (the path is not too slow). **Hold** = the old data must stay stable *after* the capture edge (the path is not too fast, so the new data doesn't race through in the same edge).

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",                "wave": "p...", "period": 4 },
  { "name": "Q1 (launch FF)",     "wave": "=....=..........", "data": ["old", "new"] },
  { "name": "D2 (after logic)",   "wave": "=....x.=........", "data": ["old", "new"] },
  { "name": "Q2 (capture FF)",    "wave": "=.........=.....", "data": ["old", "new"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "launch edge -> t_c2q -> logic -> D2 settles t_setup before the next edge; old D2 must hold t_hold after it" } }
```

| Check | Inequality (skew = capture clock arrival − launch clock arrival) |
| --- | --- |
| Setup (max delay) | `T_clk >= t_c2q + t_logic,max + t_setup - t_skew` |
| Hold (min delay) | `t_c2q + t_logic,min >= t_hold + t_skew` |

Worked numbers: `T = 1.0 ns`, `t_c2q = 0.10`, `t_setup = 0.05`, `t_logic,max = 0.90`, skew 0. Then 0.10 + 0.90 + 0.05 = 1.05 ns > 1.0, so **setup slack = −50 ps**. For hold: `t_logic,min = 0.02`, `t_hold = 0.03`, skew = +0.15. Then 0.12 < 0.18, so **hold slack = −60 ps**.

### Explanation
- **Fix setup:** pipeline the path or retime registers, reduce logic levels (restructure, precompute), upsize drivers or use low-Vt cells, improve placement, use useful skew (delay the capture clock), or lower the frequency as a last resort.
- **Fix hold:** add delay (buffers or delay cells) on the short path, or reduce skew. Frequency isn't in the hold equation, so slowing the clock does nothing.
- **Which is worse:** hold. A chip with a setup violation still works at a lower clock. A hold violation fails at every frequency, and after tape-out it can only be fixed with a metal ECO or a respin.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Positive skew (capture clock later) *helps* setup and *hurts* hold. Fixing one can break the other.
- Setup is checked at the slow corner (SS, low V, high T for most paths); hold at the fast corner (FF).
- Hold paths are often short flop-to-flop paths in scan chains or shift registers.

### Follow-ups
- *Recovery/removal?* The same checks applied to an async reset deassertion.
- *Multicycle path?* Relax setup by N cycles, and remember to adjust the hold check (`-hold N-1`).
- *Negative hold time?* Possible in a cell library: internal delay on the data pin makes the cell tolerate data changing slightly before the edge.

questions.title: Why does `assign clk = sel ? clk1 : clk2;` glitch? How do you build a glitch-free clock mux?
questions.answer:
If sel changes while the clocks are out of phase, the output can produce a runt pulse.
Fix: glitch-free mux. Each clock's enable is gated by the other's disable and synchronized on that clock's falling edge, so the old clock turns off before the new one turns on.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** a plain mux switches *immediately*. If `sel` changes while the old clock is high and the new one is low (or partway through a phase), the output gets a **runt pulse** that downstream flops may or may not see. The fix is a break-before-make handshake: the old clock is disabled on its own falling edge first, and only then is the new clock enabled on *its* falling edge.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk1",       "wave": "llhhllhhllhhllhhllhhllhh" },
  { "name": "clk2",       "wave": "lllhhhlllhhhlllhhhlllhhh" },
  { "name": "sel (1 = clk1)", "wave": "1......0................" },
  { "name": "plain mux",  "wave": "llhhllhllhhhlllhhhlllhhh" }
],
  "head": { "text": "sel switches while clk1 is high and clk2 is low: the output gets a runt high pulse" } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
module clk_mux_gf (
  input  logic clk0, clk1, rst_n, sel,     // sel = 1 selects clk1
  output logic clk_out
);
  logic en1_s, en1, en0_s, en0;
  // clk1 side: request = sel AND the other side is off
  always_ff @(posedge clk1 or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) en1_s <= 1'b0; else en1_s <= sel & ~en0;     // synchronizer stage
  always_ff @(negedge clk1 or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) en1 <= 1'b0;   else en1   <= en1_s;          // change only while clk1 is low
  // clk0 side
  always_ff @(posedge clk0 or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) en0_s <= 1'b0; else en0_s <= ~sel & ~en1;
  always_ff @(negedge clk0 or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) en0 <= 1'b0;   else en0   <= en0_s;

  assign clk_out = (clk1 & en1) | (clk0 & en0);
endmodule
```

### Explanation
- **Cross-coupling** (`& ~en0`, `& ~en1`) guarantees that both enables are never high together.
- **Negedge update:** each enable changes only while its own clock is low, so `clk & en` can't be cut in the middle of a high phase.
- The posedge flop in front of it synchronizes `sel` and the other side's enable into that clock domain (needed for unrelated clocks).
- Switching takes a few cycles of each clock, and the output is held low in between.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- If the currently selected clock **stops**, its enable can never turn off, so the mux can't switch away. That is a known limit. Use a mux with a clock-fail bypass when that matters.
- In real silicon, use the library's clock-mux / ICG cells and tell STA about both clocks (`set_clock_groups -physically_exclusive` or logically exclusive on the output).

### Follow-ups
- *Verify it:* random `sel` toggles at random phases, plus an SVA/monitor that measures every high and low pulse width of `clk_out` against the minimum of the two clocks.
- *Glitch-free clock gating?* Use an ICG: a latch transparent while the clock is low, then an AND.

questions.title: How do you avoid inferring an unintended latch?
questions.answer:
Combinational logic that doesn't assign every output on every path infers a latch.
Avoid it: default assignments at the top of always_comb, a default in every case, and use always_comb so the tool warns you.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** in combinational code, every output must be assigned on **every** path. If some path leaves a variable unassigned, it has to *remember* its old value, and the hardware for remembering without a clock is a **latch**.

```systemverilog
// BAD: y is not assigned when sel == 2'b11, and z when en == 0 -> two latches
always @(*) begin
  case (sel)
    2'b00: y = a;
    2'b01: y = b;
    2'b10: y = c;
  endcase
  if (en) z = d;
end

// GOOD: defaults first, full case, always_comb
always_comb begin
  y = '0;  z = '0;                // defaults: every path assigns y and z
  unique case (sel)
    2'b00:   y = a;
    2'b01:   y = b;
    2'b10:   y = c;
    default: y = '0;              // or a don't-care, per spec
  endcase
  if (en) z = d;
end
```

| Latch cause | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `if` without `else` | default at the top, or add `else` |
| `case` not covering all values | `default:` branch, or defaults at the top |
| output assigned in only some branches of an FSM | assign all outputs before the `case` |
| reading a variable before writing it | assign it before reading |

### Explanation
- `always_comb` tells tools that the block *must* be combinational, so lint and synthesis warn or error when a latch is inferred. `always @(*)` gives no such check.
- Default assignments at the top are the most robust habit, because new branches added later are covered automatically.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `unique case` without `default` still infers a latch if there are uncovered values. It only adds a runtime warning in simulation.
- `full_case`/`parallel_case` synthesis pragmas can hide the problem and cause simulation/synthesis mismatch. Avoid them.
- Intended latches (ICGs, time borrowing) should be written with `always_latch` so everyone knows they are deliberate.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you find latches?* Synthesis or lint reports ("Latch inferred for variable…"), or `always_comb` warnings in the simulator.
- *Why are latches bad?* They make STA harder (time borrowing), glitch-sensitive enables, and testability (scan) issues.

questions.title: Design a serial divisible-by-5 detector (bits arrive MSB first).
questions.answer:
Keep the remainder of the number seen so far. Each new bit doubles the number and adds the bit: next r = (2r + bit) mod 5, so 5 states.
Table: r0→0/1, r1→2/3, r2→4/0, r3→1/2, r4→3/4 (bit 0 / bit 1).
LSB first: the bit weights cycle 1, 2, 4, 3 (mod 5), so track (remainder, weight) = 20 states. Divisible-by-3 is the same idea with 3 states.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** don't store the number, store its **remainder mod 5**. Shifting in a bit (MSB first) gives `N' = 2N + bit`, so the remainder updates as `r' = (2r + bit) mod 5`. That's a 5-state FSM, and the output is `r == 0`.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> R0
  R0 --> R0: 0
  R0 --> R1: 1
  R1 --> R2: 0
  R1 --> R3: 1
  R2 --> R4: 0
  R2 --> R0: 1
  R3 --> R1: 0
  R3 --> R2: 1
  R4 --> R3: 0
  R4 --> R4: 1
```

| r | next r (bit = 0) | next r (bit = 1) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | 1 |
| 1 | 2 | 3 |
| 2 | 4 | 0 |
| 3 | 1 | 2 |
| 4 | 3 | 4 |

Trace for input `1 0 1 0` (= 10):

| bit in | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| number so far | 1 | 2 | 5 | 10 |
| r | 1 | 2 | 0 | 0 |
| div5 | 0 | 0 | **1** | **1** |

### Code
```systemverilog
module div5_msb (input logic clk, rst_n, din, output logic div5);
  logic [2:0] r;                         // remainder 0..4
  logic [3:0] t;
  assign t = {r, din};                   // 2r + din, at most 9
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) r <= '0;
    else        r <= (t >= 5) ? t - 4'd5 : t;   // one subtraction is enough since t <= 9
  assign div5 = (r == 0);                // number seen so far is divisible by 5
endmodule
```
Here `div5` describes the bits already shifted in (registered state). For a same-cycle answer, use `div5_now = ((t >= 5 ? t - 5 : t) == 0)`.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Decide what "no bits yet" means: after reset `r = 0`, so `div5` is 1 (0 is divisible by 5). The spec may want a valid qualifier.
- **LSB first is different:** the new bit's weight is `2^k mod 5`, which cycles 1, 2, 4, 3. Track (remainder, weight phase), which is 5 × 4 = 20 states.

### Follow-ups
- *Divisible by 3?* Same idea, 3 states: `r' = (2r + b) mod 3`.
- *Verify it:* the reference model keeps the full value (or the remainder) in the scoreboard. Use random streams plus long streams to check that nothing overflows.

questions.title: Sync vs async reset: how do you release an async reset safely? What are recovery and removal times?
questions.answer:
Sync reset: takes effect at the next edge, needs a running clock, filters glitches, logic in the data path. Async: immediate, no clock needed, a glitch can reset the flop, deassertion must meet recovery/removal.
Standard answer: assert asynchronously, deassert synchronously, with a reset synchronizer per clock domain.
Recovery = min time between reset deassertion and the next active edge (like setup). Removal = min time reset must stay asserted after an edge (like hold). Violations → metastability or flops leaving reset on different cycles.
Verify: reset mid-traffic, reset with the clock stopped, each domain reset alone.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** **assert asynchronously, deassert synchronously.** The reset takes effect at once, even with no clock, but its *release* is retimed by a 2-flop reset synchronizer, so every flop in that domain leaves reset on the same, timing-checked clock edge.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",               "wave": "p........" },
  { "name": "arst_n (async in)", "wave": "1.0..1..." },
  { "name": "rst_q1",            "wave": "1.0...1.." },
  { "name": "rst_n_sync (to flops)", "wave": "1.0....1." }
],
  "head": { "text": "assertion passes straight through; release comes 2 clock edges later, aligned to clk" } }
```

|   | Synchronous reset | Asynchronous reset |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Takes effect | at the next clock edge | immediately, no clock needed |
| Needs a running clock | yes | no (power-up, gated clocks) |
| Glitch on the reset net | mostly filtered (only sampled at the edge) | can reset the flop |
| Timing cost | reset logic sits in the data path | deassertion must meet recovery/removal |

### Code
```systemverilog
module rst_sync (input logic clk, arst_n, output logic rst_n_sync);
  logic rst_q1, rst_q2;
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge arst_n)
    if (!arst_n) {rst_q2, rst_q1} <= 2'b00;          // assert asynchronously
    else         {rst_q2, rst_q1} <= {rst_q1, 1'b1}; // release through 2 flops
  assign rst_n_sync = rst_q2;                        // drives every flop in this domain
endmodule
```

### Explanation
- **Recovery time:** the minimum time between reset *deassertion* and the next active clock edge (the reset version of setup).
- **Removal time:** the minimum time reset must stay asserted *after* a clock edge (the reset version of hold).
- If either is violated, some flops leave reset one cycle later than others (an FSM can start in an illegal state), or they go metastable. The synchronizer makes the release a normal synchronous path that STA checks.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Use one synchronizer per clock domain. Releasing several domains in a defined order may need a reset sequencer.
- Don't put logic on the reset path after the synchronizer (glitches), and don't let data-path flops without reset feed control logic.
- A reset glitch still resets the async flops. Filter it at the reset source if that's a risk.

### Follow-ups (verification angle)
- Reset in the middle of traffic: all outputs go to reset values, no X, and the scoreboard flushes its expected queues.
- Reset while the clock is stopped, which only an async reset handles.
- Reset each clock domain on its own (CDC FIFOs must recover cleanly).

questions.title: Design a valid/ready pipeline stage. Why do you need a skid buffer?
questions.answer:
A plain register slice registers valid and data, but in_ready = !out_valid || out_ready still passes ready backward combinationally; long pipelines build a long ready chain.
Skid buffer: also register ready. When the output stalls, the in-flight beat parks in a second (skid) register and in_ready drops one cycle later; no combinational path from out_ready upstream.
Checks: no beat lost or duplicated (scoreboard), out_valid held with stable data while !out_ready, one beat per cycle while out_ready stays high.
Stimulus: randomize out_ready per cycle with long stalls and single bubbles while in_valid sends bursts.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** a simple register slice breaks the forward path (`valid`, `data`) but not the backward one: `in_ready` still depends combinationally on `out_ready`. A **skid buffer** also registers `in_ready`. Because the upstream only sees the stall one cycle late, it may send one more beat, and that beat "skids" into a second register instead of being lost.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  UP["upstream"] -->|"in_valid, in_data"| SK["skid reg (skid_valid, skid_data)"]
  UP -->|"in_valid, in_data"| MX{"skid_valid ?"}
  SK --> MX
  MX --> OR["output reg (out_valid, out_data)"]
  OR --> DN["downstream"]
  DN -->|out_ready| OR
  SK -->|"in_ready = !skid_valid (from a flop)"| UP
```

Stall of 2 cycles with `in_valid` held high:
```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",        "wave": "p......." },
  { "name": "in_valid",   "wave": "1......." },
  { "name": "in_data",    "wave": "====..==", "data": ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"] },
  { "name": "in_ready",   "wave": "1..0.1.." },
  { "name": "skid_valid", "wave": "0..1.0.." },
  { "name": "skid_data",  "wave": "x..=.x..", "data": ["C"] },
  { "name": "out_valid",  "wave": "01......" },
  { "name": "out_data",   "wave": "x==..===", "data": ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"] },
  { "name": "out_ready",  "wave": "1.0.1..." }
],
  "head": { "text": "C arrives while the output stalls and parks in the skid register; in_ready drops one cycle later" } }
```

### Code
Plain register slice (full throughput, but ready is combinational):
```systemverilog
assign in_ready = !out_valid || out_ready;          // accept when empty or draining
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
  if (!rst_n)        out_valid <= 1'b0;
  else if (in_ready) out_valid <= in_valid;
always_ff @(posedge clk)
  if (in_ready && in_valid) out_data <= in_data;
```

Skid buffer (every output comes from a flop):
```systemverilog
module skid_buf #(parameter int W = 32) (
  input  logic         clk, rst_n,
  input  logic         in_valid,  output logic in_ready,
  input  logic [W-1:0] in_data,
  output logic         out_valid, input  logic out_ready,
  output logic [W-1:0] out_data
);
  logic         skid_valid, load;
  logic [W-1:0] skid_data;
  assign in_ready = !skid_valid;                    // straight from a flop
  assign load     = out_ready || !out_valid;        // output register free this cycle

  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) begin
      out_valid  <= 1'b0;
      skid_valid <= 1'b0;
    end else if (load) begin
      out_valid  <= skid_valid || in_valid;         // skid beat goes first
      skid_valid <= 1'b0;
    end else if (in_valid && in_ready) begin
      skid_valid <= 1'b1;                           // output stalled: park the beat
    end

  always_ff @(posedge clk)
    if (load)                      out_data  <= skid_valid ? skid_data : in_data;
    else if (in_valid && in_ready) skid_data <= in_data;
endmodule
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- When `load` is true and the skid register is full, `in_ready` is 0, so the skid beat goes out first and order is kept.
- `out_ready` toggling every cycle: check that no beat is duplicated or dropped and the order stays correct.
- Cost: one extra data register per stage. That is the price of breaking the ready path.

### Follow-ups (verification)
- **Checks:** a scoreboard compares the input and output beat sequences (nothing lost, duplicated or reordered); SVA `out_valid && !out_ready |=> out_valid && $stable(out_data)`; one beat per cycle while `out_ready` stays high.
- **Stimulus:** randomize `out_ready` every cycle, including long stalls and single-cycle bubbles, while `in_valid` sends bursts. Cover "skid full" and "load with skid full".

questions.title: Saturating arithmetic: clamp an 8-bit pixel add, and compute a saturating signed a×b + c.
questions.answer:
Multimedia datapaths clamp instead of wrapping (255 + 1 wrapping turns white into black).
Unsigned 8-bit add: 9-bit sum, output = sum[8] ? 8'hFF : sum[7:0].
Signed 16-bit a*b + c: compute in 33 bits, clamp to 32767 / −32768.
Width rules: N+N → N+1 bits, N×M → N+M bits, A−B of two N-bit numbers → N+1 bits (signed).
Signedness trap: one unsigned operand makes the expression unsigned; part-selects are unsigned; use $signed() on purpose.
Verify: cover results exactly at MAX/MIN, one past each, and MIN × MIN; compare with a C model that saturates the same way.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** compute in a result wide enough to never overflow, then **clamp** to the output range. Multimedia datapaths saturate because wrapping is visually catastrophic: a wrapped `255 + 1 = 0` turns a white pixel black.

| Case | Inputs | Full-width result | Output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| unsigned add | 200 + 100 | 300 (bit 8 set) | **255** |
| unsigned add | 100 + 50 | 150 | 150 |
| signed a×b+c | 200 × 200 + 0 | 40000 > 32767 | **0x7FFF** |
| signed a×b+c | −200 × 200 − 100 | −40100 < −32768 | **0x8000** |
| signed a×b+c | −32768 × −32768 + 0 | 1073741824 | **0x7FFF** |

### Code
```systemverilog
// unsigned 8-bit add, clamped
logic [7:0] a, b, pix_y;
logic [8:0] sum;                                   // one extra bit catches the carry
assign sum   = a + b;                              // context is 9 bits, so the carry is kept
assign pix_y = sum[8] ? 8'hFF : sum[7:0];

// signed 16-bit a*b + c, saturated to 16 bits
logic signed [15:0] a16, b16, c16, y16;
logic signed [32:0] full;                          // 32-bit product + 1 bit for the add
localparam logic signed [32:0] MAX = 32767, MIN = -32768;
assign full = a16 * b16 + c16;                     // all signed: operands sign-extend to 33 bits
assign y16  = (full > MAX) ? 16'sh7FFF :
              (full < MIN) ? 16'sh8000 : full[15:0];
```

### Explanation
- **Width rules:** N + N needs N+1 bits, N × M needs N+M bits, and A − B of two N-bit numbers needs N+1 bits (signed). Add one bit for every accumulation you chain.
- The expression width comes from its context (the LHS), which is why `full` is declared 33 bits *before* the multiply.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- **Signedness trap:** a single unsigned operand makes the whole expression unsigned. A part-select (`x[7:0]`) and a concatenation are always unsigned. Use `$signed()` deliberately.
- `{a + b}` inside a concatenation is self-determined (8 bits), so the carry is lost.
- Unsigned subtraction saturates at 0: `y = (a > b) ? a - b : 0`.

### Follow-ups
- *Verification:* cover results exactly at MAX and MIN, one past each, and the extreme product `MIN × MIN`. Compare against a C model that saturates the same way (bit-exact).
- *Rounding before saturation?* For a fixed-point right shift, add half an LSB first (`(x + (1 << (s-1))) >>> s`), then clamp.

questions.title: Count the number of 1s in the last W cycles (sliding window).
questions.answer:
Keep the last W bits and a running count: each cycle add the new bit and subtract the bit that falls out, so no adder tree is needed.
For a large W (e.g. 1024) use a RAM as a circular buffer: read the oldest bit and write the new one at the same pointer.
Reference model: a queue of the last W bits; cover count = 0, count = W, alternating bits.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** don't recount the window every cycle. Keep a **running count**: add the bit that enters and subtract the bit that leaves (the oldest one). That's one adder, independent of W.

Trace with W = 4 (`hist[3]` is the oldest bit):

| cycle | din | hist (after) | leaving bit | count (after) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1 | 0001 | 0 | 1 |
| 2 | 1 | 0011 | 0 | 2 |
| 3 | 0 | 0110 | 0 | 2 |
| 4 | 1 | 1101 | 0 | 3 |
| 5 | 1 | 1011 | 1 | 3 |
| 6 | 0 | 0110 | 1 | 2 |

### Code
```systemverilog
module win_count #(parameter int W = 8, localparam int CW = $clog2(W + 1)) (
  input  logic          clk, rst_n, din,
  output logic [CW-1:0] count
);
  logic [W-1:0] hist;                               // hist[W-1] is the oldest bit
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) begin
      hist  <= '0;
      count <= '0;
    end else begin
      hist  <= {hist[W-2:0], din};
      count <= count + din - hist[W-1];             // new bit in, oldest bit out
    end
endmodule
```

### Explanation
- `CW = $clog2(W+1)` because the count ranges over 0..W (W+1 values). For W = 8 that's 4 bits.
- The count can never underflow: a bit leaves only if it entered earlier and was counted.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- **Large W (e.g. 1024):** a 1024-bit shift register is big and power-hungry. Use a RAM as a circular buffer: at pointer `p`, read the oldest bit and write `din` at the same address, then `p <= p + 1`. With a 1-cycle RAM read latency, read ahead by one entry.
- Count the first W cycles after reset as "partial window" or qualify the output, depending on the spec.
- W = 1 makes `hist[W-2:0]` illegal. Handle it as a special case, or require W ≥ 2.

### Follow-ups
- *Reference model:* a SystemVerilog queue of the last W bits; `count_exp = q.sum() with (int'(item))`.
- *Coverage:* count = 0, count = W, a window of alternating bits, and a long run of 1s followed by 0s.
- *Multi-bit samples (moving sum/average)?* Same idea: `sum <= sum + x_new - x_oldest`.

questions.title: Quick checks: flip-flop vs latch, always_comb vs always @(*), `timescale, single- vs dual-port SRAM
questions.answer:
Flop captures on an edge; a latch is transparent while enable is active (smaller, allows time borrowing, harder STA; ICGs use one on purpose).
always_comb runs once at time 0, is sensitive to signals read inside called functions, and lets tools flag latches and multiple drivers; always @(*) does none of this.
`timescale 1ns/1ps: delays in ns rounded to 1 ps (#1.5 = 1.5 ns). A file without a timescale inherits the last one compiled — use timeunit/timeprecision inside the module.
Single-port SRAM: one read or one write per cycle; two-port (1R1W) or true dual-port: two. A FIFO on single-port SRAM needs arbitration or a wider, time-multiplexed memory.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** four short definitions. Each answer is one rule plus why it matters.

| Topic | Answer | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flip-flop vs latch | A flop captures D on a clock **edge**. A latch is **transparent** while its enable is active and holds otherwise. | Latches are smaller and allow time borrowing, but complicate STA and are glitch-sensitive. ICGs use one on purpose. |
| `always_comb` vs `always @(*)` | `always_comb` runs once at time 0, is sensitive to signals read inside functions it calls, forbids other blocks writing its variables, and lets tools flag latches. | `always @(*)` may not run at time 0 (outputs stay X until an input changes) and misses function-internal reads. |
| `` `timescale 1ns/1ps`` | Delays are in ns, rounded to 1 ps. `#1.5` = 1.5 ns, `#1.0004` rounds to 1.000 ns. | A file without a timescale inherits the last one compiled (or errors), a classic cross-file bug. `timeunit`/`timeprecision` inside the module avoid it. |
| Single- vs dual-port SRAM | Single-port: one read **or** one write per cycle. Two-port (1R1W): one read and one write. True dual-port: two independent R/W ports. | A FIFO on single-port SRAM needs read/write arbitration or a 2× wide, time-multiplexed memory. |

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk / en", "wave": "0.1.0.1.0." },
  { "name": "D",        "wave": "=..=.=.=..", "data": ["a", "b", "c", "d"] },
  { "name": "Q (latch, transparent while high)", "wave": "=.==..==..", "data": ["?", "a", "b", "c", "d"] },
  { "name": "Q (flop, captures at rising edge)", "wave": "=.=...=...", "data": ["?", "a", "c"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "latch follows D while en is high; flop only samples at the edge" } }
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Same-address read and write on a 1R1W SRAM: the read may return old data, new data or X, depending on the macro. Check the datasheet and model it in the testbench.
- `always_ff` / `always_comb` / `always_latch` tell lint and synthesis what you intended, and they flag code that doesn't match.

### Follow-ups
- *Why is `#1step` in a clocking block independent of the timescale?* It means one time-precision step, i.e. "just before the edge".
- *How do SRAMs handle byte writes?* With per-byte write enables (bit masks). The testbench memory model must honor them.

questions.title: What's the difference between fork…join, join_any and join_none? What does this code print?
questions.answer:
join waits for all branches, join_any for the first, join_none for none. wait fork blocks until every child of the current process finishes.
Example (#10 A, #5 B, join_any, then disable fork) prints "B @5", "after @5"; A never prints because disable fork kills it.
Trap: disable fork kills ALL children (and grandchildren) of the calling process, including ones spawned earlier with join_none. Isolate with a wrapper: fork begin ... disable fork; end join.
Killing one branch: named block + disable (kills every running instance of that block, even in other objects) or keep a process handle and call p.kill() (safer).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** the three forms differ only in **when the parent resumes**. The children always keep running unless something kills them.

| Construct | Parent resumes when | Leftover children |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fork … join` | all children finish | none |
| `fork … join_any` | any one child finishes | keep running |
| `fork … join_none` | immediately (no wait) | all keep running |

```systemverilog
initial begin
  fork
    begin #10 $display("A @%0t", $time); end
    begin #5  $display("B @%0t", $time); end
  join_any
  $display("after @%0t", $time);
  disable fork;
end
// prints:  B @5
//          after @5
// A never prints: disable fork kills it at time 5
```

### Explanation
- `wait fork;` blocks until **every** child of the current process has finished (for example, to collect `join_none` threads).
- `disable fork;` kills **every** still-running child *and grandchild* of the calling process, no matter which fork statement created it.

### The classic trap and its fix
```systemverilog
initial begin
  fork monitor_bus(); join_none          // meant to run forever

  // BUG: this disable fork also kills monitor_bus()
  fork
    wait_for_response();
    begin #1000 $error("timeout"); end
  join_any
  disable fork;
end

initial begin
  fork monitor_bus(); join_none

  fork begin                             // FIX: wrapper thread owns the race
    fork
      wait_for_response();
      begin #1000 $error("timeout"); end
    join_any
    disable fork;                        // kills only the wrapper's children
  end join
end
```
`monitor_bus()` is a *sibling* of the wrapper, not one of its descendants, so it survives.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- **Killing one specific branch:** a named block plus `disable t_a;` stops *every* running instance of that block, even in other objects of the same class. It's safer to keep a handle (`process p = process::self();`) and call `p.kill()`.
- Children that already finished are unaffected, since there's nothing left to kill.

### Follow-ups
- *With `join_none`, when do the children start?* Only when the parent blocks or finishes its current time-slot work (see the "3 3 3" loop question).
- *What does `join_any` + `disable fork` give you?* A race: the first finisher wins and the others are cancelled. It's the standard timeout pattern.

questions.title: fork/join_none inside a for loop prints 3 3 3. Why, and how do you fix it?
questions.answer:
for (int i=0;i<3;i++) fork $display(i); join_none → 3 3 3: threads only start after the loop ends, and they all read the same loop variable i (now 3).
Fix: automatic int j = i; inside the loop body before the fork → each thread gets its own copy: 0 1 2 (order not guaranteed).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `join_none` *schedules* the threads but they don't run until the parent blocks or finishes. By then the loop has finished and `i == 3`, and all three threads read the **same** variable `i`. Give each iteration its own `automatic` copy.

```systemverilog
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
  fork $display(i); join_none          // prints 3 3 3

for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) begin
  automatic int j = i;                  // fresh copy per iteration, captured at fork time
  fork $display(j); join_none           // prints 0 1 2 (order not guaranteed)
end
```

| Time-slot step | `i` | threads waiting to start | what they will print |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| iteration 0 forks | 0 | T0 | `i` (shared) |
| iteration 1 forks | 1 | T0, T1 | `i` |
| iteration 2 forks | 2 | T0, T1, T2 | `i` |
| loop exits, parent blocks | **3** | T0, T1, T2 start | 3, 3, 3 |
| with `automatic j` | — | each has its own `j` | 0, 1, 2 |

### Explanation
- The `automatic` variable must be declared **inside the loop body, outside the fork**. Its initializer runs at each iteration, so each forked thread refers to a different `j`.
- Declaring `j` inside the fork (`fork begin automatic int j = i; … end join_none`) is too late: the initializer runs when the thread starts, and `i` is already 3.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- In a `static` module context, a variable declared without `automatic` would again be shared.
- Start order of the threads is not defined by the LRM; don't depend on 0 1 2 order.
- Add `wait fork;` after the loop if the parent must wait for them all.

### Follow-ups
- *UVM use:* starting one sequence per agent in a loop: `automatic int k = i; fork seqs[k].start(sqrs[k]); join_none`.
- *Why does `fork … join` inside the loop print 0 1 2?* Because the parent waits each iteration, so each thread runs before `i` changes. But then the threads aren't parallel.

questions.title: Start three tasks in parallel and call f() as soon as any two finish. Add a timeout.
questions.answer:
Fork the three tasks with join_none, each incrementing a shared counter when done.
Then, inside an isolating wrapper (fork begin ... end join), race wait(done >= 2) against a #TIMEOUT watchdog with join_any, and disable fork (kills only the watchdog, not the third task).
Then call f(). Alternatives: a semaphore, or an event triggered by each task plus a counter.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** count completions in a shared variable, then **race** "count reached 2" against a watchdog with `join_any`. Wrap the race in its own `fork begin … end join` so the `disable fork` that cancels the loser can't kill the third, still-running task.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P["parent"] -->|join_none| T1["t1(); done++"]
  P -->|join_none| T2["t2(); done++"]
  P -->|join_none| T3["t3(); done++"]
  P --> W["wrapper thread"]
  W -->|join_any| A["wait (done >= 2)"]
  W -->|join_any| B["#TIMEOUT watchdog"]
  W -->|"first one wins, disable fork"| F["f() or error"]
```

### Code
```systemverilog
task automatic run_two_of_three(time TIMEOUT);
  int done = 0;
  bit timed_out = 0;

  fork                                   // the three tasks keep running in the background
    begin t1(); done++; end
    begin t2(); done++; end
    begin t3(); done++; end
  join_none

  fork begin                             // isolate: disable fork only sees this scope
    fork
      wait (done >= 2);
      begin #TIMEOUT; timed_out = 1; end // watchdog
    join_any
    disable fork;                        // kills the loser, not t1/t2/t3
  end join

  if (timed_out) `uvm_error("TO", "fewer than 2 tasks finished before the timeout")
  else           f();
endtask
```

### Explanation
- `done++` from several threads is safe in SystemVerilog: threads only switch at blocking points, so the increment is never interleaved.
- `wait (done >= 2)` is level-sensitive, so it can't miss the update even if two tasks finish in the same time step.
- The third task keeps running after `f()`. If it must stop, keep its `process` handle and `kill()` it, or wrap all three in another scope.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Without the wrapper, `disable fork` would also kill the third task and any other `join_none` threads the caller started earlier, such as monitors.
- Calling `f()` unconditionally after the race also calls it after a timeout. Use a flag, as above.
- If two tasks finish at exactly `TIMEOUT`, which branch wins depends on scheduling. Define the tie-break if it matters.

### Follow-ups
- *With a semaphore:* `semaphore s = new(0);` each task does `s.put(1)`, and the parent does `s.get(2)` inside the race.
- *With events:* each task triggers `ev`; the parent loops `@ev; cnt++` until `cnt == 2` (careful about two triggers in the same time step: `wait(ev.triggered)` or counters are safer).

questions.title: What's the difference between a task and a function? Static vs automatic?
questions.answer:
Function: can't consume time, returns a value (or void), can call only functions (but may start a task inside fork...join_none). Task: can consume time (#, @, wait), returns through output args, can call tasks and functions.
static: one copy of the variables shared by every call; recursion and concurrent calls corrupt each other; default in modules.
automatic: fresh variables per call (stack frame); default for class methods; needed for recursion (e.g. recursive Fibonacci).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** a **function** is zero-time and returns a value; a **task** may consume simulation time. **Static** vs **automatic** decides whether the local variables are one shared copy or a fresh copy on each call.

|   | function | task |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Consumes time (`#`, `@`, `wait`) | No | Yes |
| Return value | Yes, or `void` | Only through `output`/`ref` args |
| Can call | Functions only\* | Tasks and functions |
| Typical use | Calculations, `compare()`, `convert2string()` | Driving pins, waiting for handshakes, `body()` |

\*A function may *start* a task inside `fork … join_none`, because that doesn't block the function.

|   | static | automatic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Local variables | one copy shared by all calls | fresh copy per call (stack frame) |
| Recursion / re-entrant calls | broken | works |
| Default in | modules, interfaces, programs | class methods |

### Code
```systemverilog
module m;
  // static (default in a module): recursion corrupts n
  function automatic int fib(int n);       // 'automatic' is required for recursion
    return (n < 2) ? n : fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
  endfunction

  task automatic wait_cycles(input int n); // called from two threads at once: safe
    repeat (n) @(posedge clk);
  endtask

  initial $display("fib(10) = %0d", fib(10));   // 55
endmodule
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A static task called from two parallel threads shares its arguments and locals. The second call overwrites the first one's `n`, which is a classic testbench bug.
- Variables in a static task keep their values between calls, which is sometimes used on purpose as a counter.
- `void'(f())` discards a function's return value without a warning.

### Follow-ups
- *Can a function have output arguments?* Yes, but it still can't block.
- *Why are class methods automatic?* Many objects call the same method concurrently, so each call needs its own stack frame.

questions.title: What is polymorphism? What does this Base/Child virtual-method code print?
questions.answer:
Base has virtual show() and non-virtual hi(); Child overrides both. Base b = c (Child):
b.show() → "Child show" (virtual: dispatched on the OBJECT type); b.hi() → "Base hi" (non-virtual: dispatched on the HANDLE type).
Upcast is always legal. Why it matters in DV: one base-class handle can hold an error-injecting subclass without changing the code that uses it — the basis of UVM factory overrides.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** polymorphism means a **base-class handle** can point to a **derived object**, and calls to `virtual` methods run the derived version. Virtual methods dispatch on the *object's* type; non-virtual methods dispatch on the *handle's* type.

```systemverilog
class Base;
  virtual function void show(); $display("Base show");  endfunction
  function void hi();           $display("Base hi");    endfunction
endclass
class Child extends Base;
  virtual function void show(); $display("Child show"); endfunction
  function void hi();           $display("Child hi");   endfunction
endclass

Base b; Child c = new();
b = c;        // upcast: always legal
b.show();     // Child show   (virtual -> object type)
b.hi();       // Base hi      (non-virtual -> handle type)
c.hi();       // Child hi
```

| Call | Handle type | Object type | virtual? | Runs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `b.show()` | Base | Child | yes | **Child::show** |
| `b.hi()` | Base | Child | no | **Base::hi** |
| `c.hi()` | Child | Child | no | Child::hi |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  H["Base handle b"] --> O["Child object"]
  O -->|"virtual show()"| CS["Child::show"]
  H -->|"non-virtual hi()"| BH["Base::hi"]
```

### Why it matters in DV
- A driver, scoreboard or sequence written against `base_item` works unchanged when the test substitutes an error-injecting subclass. That is what **UVM factory overrides** rely on: `create()` returns the derived object through the base handle.
- UVM's own hooks (`do_copy`, `do_compare`, `build_phase`, `body`) are `virtual` for the same reason.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Once a method is declared `virtual`, it stays virtual in all derived classes, even without the keyword.
- An override must keep the same signature (argument types and return type).
- Calling `super.show()` inside `Child::show()` runs the base version as well.

### Follow-ups
- *Downcast?* `Child c2; $cast(c2, b);` succeeds only if `b` really points to a Child.
- *Pure virtual?* `pure virtual function void show();` in a `virtual class` forces every subclass to implement it.

questions.title: What is $cast for? What happens when it fails?
questions.answer:
$cast checks a downcast (base handle → derived handle) at run time; assigning directly is a compile error.
Used as a function: returns 1 on success, 0 on failure — always check it. Used as a task: a failure is a runtime error.
Everyday use: clone() returns uvm_object, so $cast(pkt, orig.clone()). Also int → enum conversion with a range check.

questions.title: What are an abstract (virtual) class and a singleton? When do you use them?
questions.answer:
virtual class: can't be instantiated; pure virtual methods force subclasses to implement them. Use for a common API (e.g. base_scoreboard::compare()).
Singleton: exactly one instance, reached through a static get(); constructor made local. UVM uses it for uvm_root, the factory and report servers.

questions.title: How are class handles passed to tasks and functions? Shallow vs deep copy?
questions.answer:
Handles are passed by value: the callee can change the object's fields (caller sees it), but h = new() inside the callee doesn't change the caller's handle unless the argument is ref.
b = new a; is a shallow copy: nested object handles are still shared. For a deep copy, write copy() that copies nested objects too.
SV has no overloading; overriding is polymorphic only when the method is virtual, with the same signature. C++ supports both.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** a class variable holds a **handle** (a pointer). Passing it copies the handle, not the object, so the callee and caller point to the **same** object. Re-pointing the handle inside the callee is invisible to the caller unless the argument is `ref`.

```systemverilog
class pkt; int len; hdr_c h; endclass

function void modify(pkt p);      p.len = 99;   endfunction  // caller sees 99
function void renew(pkt p);       p = new();    endfunction  // caller unchanged
function void renew_ref(ref pkt p); p = new();  endfunction  // caller's handle replaced

pkt a = new(); a.h = new();
pkt b = new a;                    // shallow copy: b.len copied, b.h == a.h (shared!)
b.h.id = 5;                       // also changes a.h.id
```

| Operation | New object? | Nested objects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `b = a;` | no (same object) | shared |
| `b = new a;` (shallow) | yes | **shared** handles |
| `b.copy(a)` / `clone()` with a deep `do_copy` | yes | copied |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Shallow["b = new a"]
    A1["a"] --> H1["hdr object"]
    B1["b (new object)"] --> H1
  end
  subgraph Deep["deep copy"]
    A2["a"] --> H2["hdr object"]
    B2["b"] --> H3["hdr copy"]
  end
```

### Deep copy
```systemverilog
function void do_copy(uvm_object rhs);
  pkt r;
  super.do_copy(rhs);
  $cast(r, rhs);
  len = r.len;
  h   = new r.h;            // copy the nested object too (or call h.copy(r.h))
endfunction
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Storing the *same* item handle in a scoreboard queue and then reusing it in the monitor overwrites the stored item. Monitors must create a new object (or clone) per transaction.
- SV has **no method overloading** (one name, one signature per class). Overriding is polymorphic only if the method is `virtual`, with the same signature. C++ supports both overloading and overriding.

### Follow-ups
- *What is `const ref`?* Pass by reference without allowing writes, which avoids copying big arrays.
- *Arrays and structs?* They are passed by value (copied) unless `ref` is used.

questions.title: Walk through the SystemVerilog scheduling regions. $display vs $strobe vs $monitor?
questions.answer:
Regions per time step: Preponed (assertion sampling) → Active (blocking, RHS of NBA, $display) → Inactive (#0) → NBA (update LHS) → Observed (assertions evaluated) → Reactive (program blocks, SVA action blocks) → Postponed ($strobe, $monitor).
$display prints immediately (Active, may show pre-NBA values); $strobe prints at the end of the time step (final values); $monitor prints whenever an argument changes, at most once per time step; $write = $display without newline.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** each simulation time step is split into ordered regions. Design code and NBA updates run first, assertions and testbench (reactive) code later, and end-of-step printing last. Which region a statement runs in decides which values it sees.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  P["Preponed: assertion / clocking-block sampling"] --> A["Active: blocking assigns, RHS of NBA, $display"]
  A --> I["Inactive: #0"]
  I --> N["NBA: update LHS of <="]
  N --> O["Observed: evaluate concurrent assertions"]
  O --> R["Reactive: program blocks, assertion action blocks"]
  R --> PP["Postponed: $strobe, $monitor"]
  N -.->|"new events loop back"| A
```

```systemverilog
initial begin
  a = 0;
  #1 a <= 1;
  $display("display a=%0d", a);   // a=0  (Active: NBA not applied yet)
  $strobe ("strobe  a=%0d", a);   // a=1  (Postponed: final value)
end
initial $monitor("monitor a=%0d at %0t", a, $time);  // prints each time step a changes
```

| Task | Region | Prints | Sees |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `$display` | Active | immediately, once | values at that moment (maybe before NBA) |
| `$write` | Active | like `$display`, no newline | same |
| `$strobe` | Postponed | once at end of time step | final settled values |
| `$monitor` | Postponed | every time step where an argument changed | final values |

### Explanation
- **Why assertions sample in Preponed:** they see the values from *before* the clock edge, so they don't race with the design's NBA updates.
- **Clocking blocks** use the same idea: inputs sampled at `#1step` (Preponed values) and outputs driven after a skew.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `$display` of a flop output in the same edge where it's updated with `<=` shows the **old** value, which confuses many people.
- Only one `$monitor` is active at a time. A new call replaces the old one (`$monitoroff`/`$monitoron` to pause).
- `#0` (Inactive) is a hack for ordering. Don't rely on it in testbenches.

### Follow-ups
- *What runs in the Re-NBA region?* Non-blocking assignments made by reactive (program/testbench) code.
- *Why did `program` blocks exist?* To run the testbench in the Reactive region, after the design settles. Clocking blocks mostly replace that need.

questions.title: Why use a clocking block and a virtual interface in a testbench?
questions.answer:
Clocking block: TB samples inputs at #1step (Preponed value) and drives outputs after a skew, removing TB/DUT races at the clock edge. modport fixes directions for each side.
Virtual interface: an interface is a static hardware instance and classes are dynamic; a class can't contain an interface but can hold a handle to one (virtual my_if vif), usually passed through uvm_config_db.

questions.title: What's the difference between logic, wire and reg? Can logic replace wire everywhere?
questions.answer: logic is 4-state and can take one procedural or one continuous driver. It can't replace wire where there are multiple drivers (tri-state bus, inout), because only nets resolve multiple drivers.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `logic` is a 4-state **variable** type that may be written either procedurally or by a single continuous assignment. `wire` is a **net**: it can have many drivers and resolves them (0 vs Z, 0 vs 1 → X). So `logic` replaces `reg` everywhere and `wire` almost everywhere, except where there are **multiple drivers**.

|   | `reg` (Verilog) | `logic` (SV) | `wire` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Kind | variable | variable | net |
| States | 4 | 4 | 4 (resolved) |
| Written by | procedural blocks only | procedural **or** one `assign`/port | `assign`, ports, multiple drivers |
| Multiple drivers | no | **no** (compile error) | yes, resolved |
| Holds a value without a driver | yes | yes | no (Z) |
| Typical use | old-style flop/comb outputs | almost everything in SV | tri-state, `inout`, wired logic |

```systemverilog
module tri_bus (inout wire data, input logic en_a, en_b, a, b);
  assign data = en_a ? a : 1'bz;     // driver 1
  assign data = en_b ? b : 1'bz;     // driver 2: legal only because data is a net
endmodule
// logic data;  + the two assigns above -> error: multiple continuous drivers
```

### Explanation
- `reg` never meant "register". It only meant "assigned in a procedural block". `logic` removes the confusion.
- `bit` is the 2-state version (0/1 only). It's faster in testbenches but hides X: an X becomes 0.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `inout` ports and open-drain buses (I2C) must be nets (`wire`, `tri1` for a pull-up).
- With `logic`, a second driver is reported at compile time, which actually catches bugs that `wire` would silently resolve to X.

### Follow-ups
- *`wire logic`?* Legal: a net with explicit logic data type (the default net type).
- *`default_nettype none`?* Turns implicit nets into errors, so a typo doesn't create a silent 1-bit wire.

questions.title: Mailbox vs queue vs associative array: when do you use each?
questions.answer:
Mailbox: blocking get() between threads (monitor → checker), thread-safe. Queue [$]: ordered FIFO inside one class, e.g. in-order scoreboard. Associative array [key]: sparse lookup by ID or address, e.g. out-of-order scoreboard or sparse memory model.
Bounded mailbox new(N) blocks put() when full → backpressure. Semaphore new(1) with get(1)/put(1) gives mutual exclusion (e.g. two threads sharing one bus).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** pick the container by **access pattern**: thread-to-thread hand-off with blocking (mailbox), ordered storage inside one component (queue), or lookup by a sparse key (associative array).

| Container | Ordering | Blocking? | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `mailbox #(T)` | FIFO | `get()`/`put()` block (bounded) | monitor thread → checker thread |
| queue `T q[$]` | ordered, push/pop both ends | no | in-order scoreboard, history buffers |
| assoc array `T aa[key]` | by key (sparse) | no | out-of-order scoreboard by ID, sparse memory model |
| `semaphore` | — | `get()` blocks | mutual exclusion on a shared resource |

```systemverilog
mailbox #(pkt) mb = new(4);          // bounded: put() blocks when 4 items are waiting
pkt          exp_q[$];               // in-order expected queue
bit [31:0]   mem [bit [31:0]];       // sparse memory: only written addresses exist
pkt          by_id [int][$];         // ID -> in-order queue (out-of-order scoreboard)
semaphore    bus_lock = new(1);      // one key

// producer / consumer
fork
  forever begin pkt p = new(); /* fill */ mb.put(p); end   // backpressure when full
  forever begin pkt p; mb.get(p); check(p); end            // blocks until data arrives
join_none

// mutual exclusion
bus_lock.get(1); drive_bus(); bus_lock.put(1);

// memory model read with a default
function bit [31:0] rd(bit [31:0] a); return mem.exists(a) ? mem[a] : '0; endfunction
```

### Explanation
- A **mailbox** is safe between threads and lets the consumer sleep until data arrives. A queue has no blocking `get`, so polling it needs `wait (q.size() > 0)`.
- **Bounded** mailbox: `put()` blocks when full, which gives the producer backpressure.
- Associative arrays only allocate entries that were written, which suits a 4 GB address space.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Reading a non-existent associative-array key returns the default value with a warning. Check `exists()` first.
- `mailbox` without a type parameter accepts anything, and a `get()` into the wrong type fails at run time. Use `mailbox #(T)`.
- In UVM, `uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo` usually replaces raw mailboxes between components.

### Follow-ups
- *`try_get()` / `peek()`?* Non-blocking get, and a look without removing.
- *Dynamic array vs queue?* A dynamic array is resized explicitly (`new[n]`) and is fast for indexing; a queue grows and shrinks at the ends.

questions.title: Use the streaming operator to reverse bits, reverse bytes, and flatten an array.
questions.answer:
rev_bits = {<<{x}}; rev_bytes = {<<8{x}} (endian swap); flat = {>>{arr2d}} packs an unpacked array into a vector.
Example: x = 8'b1101_0010 → 8'b0100_1011; 32'h12345678 → 32'h78563412; 2x2 bytes 11,22,33,44 → 32'h11223344.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `{>>{…}}` streams the bits left to right (MSB first) unchanged; `{<<N{…}}` streams them in **slices of N bits in reverse order**. N = 1 reverses bits, N = 8 swaps bytes. The same operator packs and unpacks arrays.

| Expression | Input | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `{<<{x}}` (bit reverse) | `8'b1101_0010` | `8'b0100_1011` |
| `{<<8{w}}` (byte swap) | `32'h12_34_56_78` | `32'h78_56_34_12` |
| `{>>{arr2d}}` (flatten) | `arr2d = '{'{8'h11, 8'h22}, '{8'h33, 8'h44}}` | `32'h11_22_33_44` |
| `{<<4{w}}` (nibble reverse) | `16'hABCD` | `16'hDCBA` |

### Code
```systemverilog
module streaming_example;
  logic [7:0]  x, rev_bits;
  logic [31:0] word_in, rev_bytes, flat;
  logic [7:0]  arr2d [0:1][0:1];        // 2 x 2 unpacked array of bytes
  logic [7:0]  bytes_q [$];

  initial begin
    x         = 8'b1101_0010;
    rev_bits  = {<<{x}};                 // 8'b0100_1011
```
