```systemverilog
    word_in   = 32'h12_34_56_78;
    rev_bytes = {<<8{word_in}};          // 32'h78_56_34_12
    arr2d     = '{'{8'h11, 8'h22}, '{8'h33, 8'h44}};
    flat      = {>>{arr2d}};             // 32'h11_22_33_44
    bytes_q   = {>>8{word_in}};          // unpack: '{8'h12, 8'h34, 8'h56, 8'h78}
    $display("rev_bits=%b rev_bytes=%h flat=%h", rev_bits, rev_bytes, flat);
  end
endmodule
```

### Explanation
- On the right-hand side the operator **packs** a stream; on the left-hand side (`{>>{a, b}} = vec;`) it **unpacks** a vector into variables or arrays.
- Packets in a TB: `{>>byte{pkt_bytes}} = {hdr, payload, crc};` serializes a transaction to bytes for a driver.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- If the target is wider than the stream, the result is left-aligned and padded with zeros on the right. If the stream is wider than the target, it's an error.
- With `<<N` and a width that isn't a multiple of N, the last slice is shorter. Check the result.

### Follow-ups
- *Without the operator?* A `for` loop: `for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) r[i] = x[7-i];`.
- *Endianness in a scoreboard?* Byte-swap with `{<<8{}}` when the bus is little-endian and the model is big-endian.

questions.title: case vs casez vs casex; unique vs priority case
questions.answer:
case: exact 4-state match (X/Z must match literally). casez: Z and ? are don't-cares in items AND in the case expression — the usual way to write a priority encoder. casex: X is a don't-care too, so an X on the selector silently matches and hides bugs; avoid it.
unique case: exactly one item must match (warns on overlap or no match; synthesis may build parallel logic). priority case: first match wins, warns if nothing matches. unique0 allows no match.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `case`, `casez` and `casex` differ in which bits count as **don't-care**. `unique`/`priority` are **assertions plus synthesis hints** about how many items can match.

| Form | Don't-care bits | Danger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `case` | none: 0/1/X/Z must match exactly | X on the selector matches only an explicit X item |
| `casez` | `Z` and `?` in items **and** in the selector | a Z on the selector matches anything |
| `casex` | `X`, `Z`, `?` in items and selector | an X on the selector silently matches the first item and **hides bugs**: avoid |

```systemverilog
always_comb begin
  casez (req)                         // priority encoder: first match wins
    4'b???1: gnt = 4'b0001;
    4'b??10: gnt = 4'b0010;
    4'b?100: gnt = 4'b0100;
    4'b1000: gnt = 4'b1000;
    default: gnt = 4'b0000;
  endcase
end
```

| Modifier | Simulation check | Synthesis meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `unique case` | warning if **0 or more than 1** item matches | items are mutually exclusive: parallel mux, no priority chain |
| `unique0 case` | warning if more than 1 matches (no match is OK) | same, no-match allowed |
| `priority case` | warning if **no** item matches | evaluate in order; all cases covered |

### Explanation
- `unique` lets synthesis build a flat, parallel mux. If the items actually overlap, synthesis and simulation disagree, which is why the simulator checks it at run time.
- `priority` keeps the order (first match wins) but promises that some item always matches.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `casex` with an X selector picks a branch in RTL, but gates propagate X. This is classic X-optimism that only shows up in gate-level simulation.
- `unique case` without `default` can still infer a latch for unlisted values.
- Prefer `case (…) inside` for wildcards: `4'b1???` works with `?` in items only, so the selector's X/Z are not treated as wildcards.

### Follow-ups
- *Old pragmas?* `// synopsys full_case parallel_case` change only synthesis, so they cause sim/synth mismatches. `unique`/`priority` replace them safely.

questions.title: SystemVerilog gotchas interviewers like: == vs ===, assert(randomize()), $random vs $urandom, part-selects, lost carry
questions.answer:
== returns X if either side has X/Z; === compares X/Z literally (always 0/1); ==? treats X/Z in the right operand as wildcards. if (sig == 1'bx) is never true → use $isunknown.
assert(tr.randomize()): if assertions are disabled, randomize() is skipped too → use if (!tr.randomize()) `uvm_error.
$random: signed, one shared generator, not thread-stable. $urandom / $urandom_range(max,min): unsigned, per-thread RNG → stable when other threads change.
Variable part-select: data[i*8 +: 8] / data[i*8+7 -: 8]; data[i*8+7 : i*8] doesn't compile (width must be constant).
Lost carry: sum = {a + b} — operand inside a concatenation is self-sized; sum = a + b with a wider sum keeps it.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** most SV gotchas come from **X semantics**, **expression sizing**, and **random stability**. Know each rule and the safe alternative.

| Gotcha | What goes wrong | Safe form |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `if (sig == 1'bx)` | `==` with X/Z returns X, so the condition is never true | `if ($isunknown(sig))` or `sig === 1'bx` |
| `==` vs `===` vs `==?` | `==` → X on unknowns; `===` matches X/Z literally (always 0/1); `==?` treats X/Z in the **right** operand as wildcards | choose deliberately |
| `assert(tr.randomize());` | `$assertoff` or `-noassert` also skips the call, so nothing is randomized | `if (!tr.randomize()) `uvm_error("RND", "failed")` |
| `$random` | signed, one global stream: adding a thread changes everyone's values | `$urandom`, `$urandom_range(max, min)` |
| `data[i*8+7 : i*8]` | variable range width: compile error | `data[i*8 +: 8]` or `data[i*8+7 -: 8]` |
| `sum = {a + b};` | the concatenation operand is self-sized, so the carry is lost | `sum = a + b;` with a wider `sum` |

Random stability, illustrated:
```text
$random (one shared stream)             $urandom (one stream per thread)
      global seed                             root RNG (from the seed)
     /    |     \                             seeds each child at creation
   T1    T2     T3                          RNG_1    RNG_2    RNG_3
  all pull from the same stream               |        |        |
  -> values depend on call order             T1       T2       T3
```

```systemverilog
initial begin : A  repeat (3) $display("A: %0d", $urandom); end
initial begin : B  repeat (3) $display("B: %0d", $urandom); end
// Add a 4th $urandom call in B, or a new thread C:
//   $urandom -> A prints exactly the same values (its own seeded stream)
//   $random  -> A's values may change (B consumed numbers from the shared stream)
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `==?` only treats the **right** operand's X/Z as wildcards: `4'b1010 ==? 4'b1x1x` is 1.
- `$urandom_range(max, min)`: the argument order is max first, and the min defaults to 0.
- In UVM, objects created in a different order also shift random streams. Create objects in a stable order and seed key objects (`srandom`).

### Follow-ups
- *Why is `$urandom` thread-stable?* Each thread and object has its own RNG, seeded from its parent when it's created (hierarchical seeding).
- *`!==`?* The case-inequality operator, the negation of `===`.

questions.title: Spot the bugs in this UVM driver and sequence code
questions.answer: 1) my_if vif → must be virtual my_if vif. 2) Missing `uvm_component_utils(my_driver) → factory can't create/override. 3) config_db get() result not checked → use uvm_fatal. 4) run_phase declared as a function but waits on the clock → must be a task. 5) No item_done() → finish_item never returns, test hangs. 6) my_seq has no new(string name) → utils macro won't compile. 7) Item built with new() instead of type_id::create(), and never randomized between start_item and finish_item. 8) build_phase should call super.build_phase(phase).

questions.title: C/C++ quick checks: const pointers, pass by value/pointer/reference, virtual destructor, memcpy vs memmove, struct vs class
questions.answer:
const int *p: can't change the value through p but can repoint; int *const p: can't repoint but can change the value.
Pass by value copies; swap needs pointers or references; const T& avoids a copy without allowing changes.
A base class used through base pointers needs a virtual destructor, else delete base_ptr skips the derived destructor (UB, usually a leak).
memcpy on overlapping buffers is UB → memmove; always check the size against the destination.
C++ struct vs class: only the default access differs (public vs private).

questions.title: What happens during a single randomize() call?
questions.answer:
1) pre_randomize() runs. 2) The solver finds one solution satisfying every active constraint over the active rand/randc variables (constraint_mode(0) / rand_mode(0) switch some off). 3) post_randomize() runs. 4) Returns 1; on failure returns 0 and leaves the variables unchanged — always check it.
Inline constraints (randomize() with {...}) add to class constraints; they can't loosen them. std::randomize(x) with {...} randomizes non-member variables.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `randomize()` is *pre-hook → constraint solve → post-hook → status*. The solver treats every **active** constraint as a hard requirement (except `soft` ones) and picks one solution from the legal set.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["obj.randomize() with {...}"] --> B["pre_randomize()"]
  B --> C["solver: active rand/randc vars + active class constraints + inline constraints"]
  C --> D{"solution exists?"}
  D -->|yes| E["assign values, post_randomize(), return 1"]
  D -->|no| F["variables unchanged, post_randomize() skipped, return 0"]
```

### Explanation
- **Active variables:** `rand` and `randc` members whose `rand_mode` is on, including those of `rand` member objects, recursively. Everything else is a *state variable*, treated as a constant.
- **Active constraints:** class constraints with `constraint_mode(1)`, plus the inline `with {…}` block, which can only **add** restrictions. A conflict with a hard class constraint fails the call.
- `pre_randomize()` is the place to set up state (e.g. copy the last value). `post_randomize()` computes derived fields such as CRC or parity.

```systemverilog
class pkt;
  rand bit [7:0] len;
  rand bit [7:0] payload[];
       bit [7:0] crc;
  constraint c_len  { len inside {[1:64]}; }
  constraint c_size { payload.size() == len; }
  function void post_randomize(); crc = calc_crc(payload); endfunction
endclass

pkt p = new();
if (!p.randomize() with { len < 8; }) `uvm_error("RND", "randomize failed")
p.c_len.constraint_mode(0);            // switch a constraint off
p.len.rand_mode(0); p.len = 100;       // treat len as a fixed state variable
int x;  if (!std::randomize(x) with { x inside {[0:9]}; }) $error("fail");
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- **Always check the return value.** A failed call leaves the *previous* values in place, so the test silently re-sends the old transaction.
- Don't wrap it in `assert(...)`: disabling assertions also removes the call.
- `randc` cycles through all values before repeating, per object, and only for that variable.

### Follow-ups
- *Debug a failing randomize?* Turn constraints off one at a time, or use the simulator's solver debug (e.g. `+ntb_solver_debug` in VCS) to print the conflicting set.
- *Why are sizes solved first?* Array `size()` must be fixed before element constraints can be built.

questions.title: What do inside, dist and solve…before do? Does solve…before change the legal solutions?
questions.answer:
dist: := gives the weight to EACH value; :/ SPLITS the weight across the range. Example len dist {0 := 1, [1:3] := 2, [4:15] :/ 7}.
solve a before b changes only the probability distribution, never the legal set. Example: bit mode; bit [7:0] len; mode -> len == 0. Without ordering, 257 legal pairs are equally likely, so P(mode=1) = 1/257; with solve mode before len, P(mode=1) = 1/2. randc variables can't appear in solve...before.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `inside` restricts the **legal set**; `dist` and `solve…before` only reshape the **probabilities** within it.

```systemverilog
constraint c_len {
  len inside {[0:15]};
  len dist { 0 := 1, [1:3] := 2, [4:15] :/ 7 };
  // :=  weight applies to EACH value:   0 -> 1;  1, 2, 3 -> 2 each
  // :/  weight is SPLIT over the range: 4..15 share 7 in total
}
```

| Value | Weight | Probability (total weight 14) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 1 | 1/14 ≈ 7.1% |
| 1, 2, 3 | 2 each | 2/14 ≈ 14.3% each |
| 4 … 15 | 7/12 each | ≈ 4.2% each (50% together) |

### solve…before
```systemverilog
rand bit       mode;
rand bit [7:0] len;
constraint c_dep { mode -> len == 0; }
constraint c_ord { solve mode before len; }
```

| | Legal (mode, len) pairs | P(mode = 1) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| no ordering | 256 with mode = 0, plus 1 with mode = 1 = **257**, all equally likely | 1/257 |
| `solve mode before len` | the same 257 pairs | **1/2** (mode is picked first, uniformly) |

### Explanation
- The default solver is uniform over **all legal solutions together**, so a rarely-legal value of one variable becomes rare.
- `solve a before b` makes the solver pick `a` first (uniformly over its feasible values), then `b` given `a`. The legal set doesn't change.
- `dist` is a soft weighting, not a hard limit: values outside the `dist` list are still legal unless another constraint excludes them. Pair it with `inside` if needed.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `randc` variables can't appear in `solve…before`, because they're always solved first anyway.
- `dist` can't be used on `randc` variables.
- Weight 0 (`5 := 0`) excludes a value from the distribution.

### Follow-ups
- *Another way to get 50/50 mode?* `mode dist {0 := 1, 1 := 1};` gives the same effect here.
- *Implication vs if-else?* `a -> b` is the same as `if (a) b;`, and both are bidirectional for the solver.

questions.title: Make array elements unique without using the unique keyword.
questions.answer:
Pairwise constraint: foreach (arr[i]) foreach (arr[j]) if (i < j) arr[i] != arr[j]; (O(N^2) constraints).
Alternative: fill 0..N-1 (or any distinct set) in post_randomize() and call arr.shuffle() — O(N), and also a way to get randc-like behavior without randc.

questions.title: Constrain a dynamic array so that its elements sum to 20.
questions.answer:
rand bit [7:0] da[]; constraint c_size { da.size() inside {[4:8]}; } constraint c_sum { da.sum() with (int'(item)) == 20; }
Trap: sum() computes at the element width, so 8-bit values can overflow and wrap; the int'(item) cast fixes it.
The size is solved before the elements — always bound size().
Count matching elements: da.sum() with (int'(item > 200)) >= 2. Resize and keep data: da = new[16](da).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** constrain the **size** (bounded!) and the **sum**, and widen the sum so it can't overflow at the element width.

```systemverilog
class sum20;
  rand bit [7:0] da[];
  constraint c_size { da.size() inside {[4:8]}; }               // always bound the size
  constraint c_sum  { da.sum() with (int'(item)) == 20; }       // sum in 32 bits
endclass
```

Why the cast matters: without it, the sum is computed at 8 bits.

| da | true sum | 8-bit `sum()` | passes `== 20` without cast? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 5, 5, 5, 5 | 20 | 20 | yes (correct) |
| 200, 76, 0, 0 | 276 | 276 mod 256 = **20** | **yes (wrong!)** |
| 255, 255, 22, 0 | 532 | 532 mod 256 = **20** | **yes (wrong!)** |

With `int'(item)` the sum is 32 bits, so only true sums of 20 pass.

### Explanation
- The solver fixes `size()` first, then solves the elements. An unbounded size can make the solver pick huge arrays or fail.
- `with (expr)` maps each element before summing. It works for counting too:
```systemverilog
constraint c_cnt  { da.sum() with (int'(item > 200)) >= 2; }   // at least two elements > 200
constraint c_even { da.sum() with (int'(item[0] == 0)) == da.size(); }  // all even
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `item` is the implicit iterator name; `da.sum(x) with (int'(x))` names it explicitly.
- `product()` overflows even faster: cast to `longint` and bound the elements.
- To resize at run time and keep the old data: `da = new[16](da);`.

### Follow-ups
- *Each element non-zero?* `foreach (da[i]) da[i] > 0;` (then size ≤ 20).
- *Sum of a 2-D array?* Constrain each row's sum, then a separate sum over a helper array of row sums.

questions.title: Randomize a 16-bit value that has exactly one run of consecutive 1s.
questions.answer:
Randomize start position and length, then derive x: len in [1:16], start in [0:15], start + len <= 16, x == ((17'h1 << len) - 1) << start.
Bit-trick check: x is one contiguous run iff x != 0 and x + (x & -x) is a power of 2 (computed in 17 bits).
One-hot without $countones: x != 0; (x & (x-1)) == 0. Exactly N ones: helper rand bit b[16], b.sum() with (int'(item)) == N, pack into x.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** describe the shape, not the bits. A single run of 1s is fully defined by **where it starts** and **how long it is**, so randomize those two and derive `x`.

```systemverilog
class one_run;
  rand bit [15:0]   x;
  rand int unsigned start, len;
  constraint c_run {
    len   inside {[1:16]};
    start inside {[0:15]};
    start + len <= 16;
    x == ((17'h1 << len) - 1) << start;    // len ones, shifted up by start
  }
endclass
```

Worked example: `start = 3`, `len = 4` → `(1 << 4) - 1 = 0b1111` → `<< 3` → `x = 16'b0000_0000_0111_1000` (0x0078).

Bit-trick check (handy in a checker or as a follow-up):

| x | `x & -x` (lowest 1) | `x + (x & -x)` | power of 2? | one run? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0111_1000 | 0000_1000 | 1000_0000 | yes | yes |
| 0101_1000 | 0000_1000 | 0110_0000 | no | no |
| 1111_1111_1111_1111 | 1 | 1_0000_0000_0000_0000 (17 bits) | yes | yes |

Adding the lowest set bit makes a contiguous run carry all the way through, leaving a single 1. Compute it in 17 bits so the all-ones case doesn't wrap to 0.

### Related patterns
```systemverilog
constraint c_onehot { x != 0; (x & (x - 1)) == 0; }       // one-hot without $countones

rand bit b[16];                                           // exactly N ones, without $countones
constraint c_n  { b.sum() with (int'(item)) == N; }
function void post_randomize(); foreach (b[i]) x[i] = b[i]; endfunction
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `start + len <= 16` uses `int unsigned`, which can't wrap here because both are bounded. Always bound helper variables.
- The distribution is uniform over (start, len) pairs, so short runs are more common than in a uniform choice over all legal `x` values. Add `solve` or `dist` if that matters.

### Follow-ups
- *Exactly two runs?* Two (start, len) pairs with a gap of at least 1 between them.
- *Run of 0s?* Constrain `~x` the same way.

questions.title: Randomize non-overlapping memory regions (aligned, inside a 1 KB space).
questions.answer:
rand int unsigned base[4], size[4]; bound base < 1024, size in [1:64], base % 32 == 0, base + size <= 1024; for every pair i<j: (base[i]+size[i] <= base[j]) || (base[j]+size[j] <= base[i]).
Watch wrap-around: with bit [9:0], base+size wraps at 1024; with an unbounded int unsigned, a base near 2^32 wraps too. Either way an out-of-range or overlapping region can pass, so bound base explicitly.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** two regions don't overlap when **one ends before the other starts**. Constrain every pair with that OR, and bound every value so the additions can't wrap.

```systemverilog
class mem_regions;
  rand int unsigned base[4], size[4];
  constraint c_region {
    foreach (base[i]) {
      base[i] < 1024;                    // bound it, or base + size can wrap at 2^32
      size[i] inside {[1:64]};
      base[i] % 32 == 0;                 // 32-byte aligned
      base[i] + size[i] <= 1024;         // stay inside 1 KB
    }
    foreach (base[i]) foreach (base[j])
      if (i < j) (base[i] + size[i] <= base[j]) || (base[j] + size[j] <= base[i]);
  }
endclass
```

One possible solution:

| region | base | size | end (exclusive) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0x060 | 40 | 0x088 |
| 1 | 0x200 | 64 | 0x240 |
| 2 | 0x000 | 17 | 0x011 |
| 3 | 0x3E0 | 32 | 0x400 |

```text
0x000 [2]--)    0x060 [0]----)        0x200 [1]------)          0x3E0 [3]---) 0x400
```

### Explanation
- `(end_i <= start_j) || (end_j <= start_i)` is the standard interval non-overlap test, with ends exclusive.
- The `i < j` guard avoids comparing a region with itself (which would be unsatisfiable) and halves the constraints.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- **Wrap-around:** if `base` and `size` were both `bit [9:0]`, then 1000 + 40 would wrap to 16 and pass the checks. With unbounded `int unsigned`, a base near 2^32 wraps the same way. Either way an out-of-range or overlapping region slips through, so bound `base` explicitly.
- Too many regions or sizes for the space makes the constraint unsatisfiable. Check the randomize result.

### Follow-ups
- *Sorted regions?* Add `base[i] + size[i] <= base[i+1]` for consecutive i instead of all pairs (O(N) constraints).
- *Allow touching but not overlapping?* That's already the case (`<=`). Use `<` to require a gap.

questions.title: How do you override a parent class constraint in a child class? Give three methods.
questions.answer:
1) Same constraint name in the child replaces the parent's. 2) Turn it off: tr.c_len.constraint_mode(0), then add new constraints inline. 3) Make it soft in the parent: constraint c_len { soft len < 16; } so an inline with {len == 100;} wins instead of failing.
An inline with can't relax a hard constraint; a conflict makes randomize() return 0.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** constraints are **inherited like virtual methods by name**, can be **switched off** per object, and `soft` constraints **give way** to any conflicting hard constraint.

```systemverilog
class base_tr;
  rand bit [7:0] len;
  constraint c_len  { len inside {[1:15]}; }
  constraint c_def  { soft len < 8; }               // method 3: soft default
endclass

class long_tr extends base_tr;                      // method 1: same name replaces it
  constraint c_len { len inside {[100:200]}; }
endclass

base_tr t = new();
t.c_len.constraint_mode(0);                         // method 2: turn it off for this object
if (!t.randomize() with { len == 250; }) `uvm_error("RND", "failed")
// c_def (soft) yields to the inline len == 250
```

| Method | Scope | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Same name in the child | every object of the child class | parent's `c_len` replaced |
| `constraint_mode(0)` | one object, at run time | constraint ignored until turned back on |
| `soft` in the parent | wherever it conflicts | dropped silently when a hard constraint disagrees |

### Explanation
- A child constraint with a **different** name is *added* to the parent's, so both must hold.
- `soft` constraints are resolved by priority: later and more specific (inline, child) beats earlier (parent).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- An inline `with {}` **can't relax** a hard constraint: `with { len == 250; }` while `c_len` (1..15) is active makes `randomize()` return 0.
- Calling `constraint_mode(0)` on a name that doesn't exist is a compile error. Calling it on the class handle affects only that object.
- In UVM, a factory override to `long_tr` changes the constraints for every item a sequence creates, with no change to the sequence.

### Follow-ups
- *Disable all constraints?* `t.constraint_mode(0);` on the object.
- *Turn off randomization of one field?* `t.len.rand_mode(0);`.

questions.title: Randomize a 300-element array with values 0–5, each appearing exactly 50 times, and no two 0s in a row.
questions.answer:
rand bit [2:0] arr[300]; each element inside [0:5]; for each value v: arr.sum() with (int'(item == v)) == 50; foreach i>0: !(arr[i] == 0 && arr[i-1] == 0).
With this many elements the solver gets slow. For performance build the multiset in post_randomize(), shuffle it, and repair any 0–0 pairs.

questions.title: Constrain a dynamic array so that any 5 consecutive values are all different (sliding window).
questions.answer: foreach (da[i]) if (i + 4 < da.size()) unique {da[i], da[i+1], da[i+2], da[i+3], da[i+4]};

questions.title: More constraint patterns: strictly increasing array, alternating read/write transactions, Sudoku
questions.answer:
Strictly increasing: foreach (a[i]) if (i > 0) a[i] > a[i-1].
Alternate READ/WRITE across randomize calls: keep the last value in a static variable, constrain is_wr != last_wr, update it in post_randomize.
Sudoku: g[r][c] inside [1:9]; each row unique; for every pair of cells in the same column or same 3x3 box (r < r2), values differ.

questions.title: What does the solver do when you call a function inside a constraint?
questions.answer:
Random variables passed as function arguments are solved BEFORE the function runs (an implicit solve-before); the function result is only checked afterwards, so count_big(a) == 2 usually fails.
Use an array method the solver handles in both directions: a.sum() with (int'(item > 100)) == 2.
Functions in constraints can't have output or ref arguments (const ref is fine) and shouldn't have side effects.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** the solver can't "see inside" a function. Random arguments are solved **first**, as if with `solve args before result`, then the function is evaluated once and the constraint is just checked. The solver can't steer the arguments to make the result come out right.

```systemverilog
rand bit [7:0] a[8];

constraint c_sym { foreach (a[i]) if (i < 4) a[i] == a[7-i]; }   // relations: no function needed

function int count_big(bit [7:0] arr[8]);
  int n = 0;
  foreach (arr[i]) if (arr[i] > 100) n++;
  return n;
endfunction
constraint c_fn  { count_big(a) == 2; }                          // RISKY: usually fails

constraint c_ok  { a.sum() with (int'(item > 100)) == 2; }       // solver understands this
```

| Step | With `count_big(a) == 2` | With `a.sum() with (...) == 2` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | solve `a` with no knowledge of the target | build one combined problem over `a` |
| 2 | evaluate `count_big(a)`, e.g. 4 | solver picks `a` so exactly 2 elements are > 100 |
| 3 | 4 != 2: **randomize fails** (or retries, tool-dependent) | success |

### Explanation
- Functions are fine for things that depend only on **state variables** or on variables solved earlier on purpose, e.g. `len == calc_len(mode)` where `mode` should be picked first.
- Array reduction methods (`sum`, `product`, `and`, `or`, `xor` with `with`) and `foreach` are expanded into real constraints, so they work in both directions.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Functions called in constraints can't have `output` or `ref` arguments (`const ref` is fine) and shouldn't have side effects. They may be called several times.
- The implicit ordering can create circular-dependency errors if two functions use each other's results.
- `$countones(x)` is understood by most solvers, but interviewers often ban it. Know the `sum()` form.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you check symmetry with a function safely?* Call the function in `post_randomize()` as a self-check, not as a constraint.

questions.title: What's the difference between an immediate and a concurrent assertion?
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** an **immediate** assertion is a procedural `if` that reports an error, evaluated once, right now. A **concurrent** assertion is a temporal property, clocked, sampled race-free in the Preponed region, and able to span many cycles.

|   | Immediate | Concurrent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where | inside procedural code: `assert (x);` | stand-alone (module, interface, checker): `assert property (...)` |
| Timing | evaluated when the statement executes | sampled in Preponed, evaluated in Observed, every clock |
| Spans cycles | no | yes (`##`, `[*]`, `$past`, `|=>`) |
| Typical use | `randomize()` result, scoreboard values, function arguments | protocol rules on DUT signals |
| Formal tools | rarely | yes (assert / assume / cover) |

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",   "wave": "p....." },
  { "name": "req",   "wave": "01.0.." },
  { "name": "gnt",   "wave": "0.10.." },
  { "name": "assert property: req |=> gnt", "wave": "x.=x..", "data": ["pass @3"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "a concurrent assertion samples req at edge 2 and checks gnt at edge 3" } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
// immediate: procedural
always_comb assert (!(rd_en && wr_en)) else $error("simultaneous rd/wr");
if (!tr.randomize()) `uvm_error("RND", "fail")   // preferred over assert(tr.randomize())

// concurrent: temporal, clocked
module fifo_sva (input logic clk, rst_n, full, wr_en);
  a_no_overflow: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) full |-> !wr_en);
endmodule

// attach to the RTL without editing it
bind sync_fifo fifo_sva u_sva (.*);
```

### Explanation
- **Deferred immediate** assertions (`assert #0` / `assert final`) wait until the end of the time step, which avoids false failures from zero-delay glitches in `always_comb`.
- `bind` instantiates the checker module inside every instance (or one instance) of the DUT module, so verification code stays out of the RTL files.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A concurrent assertion inside a class is illegal. Put it in the interface or a bound checker.
- Immediate assertions in `always_comb` can fire on transient values during delta cycles. Use deferred ones.

### Follow-ups
- *Can a concurrent assertion be placed in procedural code?* Yes, as a *procedural concurrent* assertion inside `always @(posedge clk)`; it inherits the clock and the enclosing `if` condition.

questions.title: What's the difference between |-> and |=>? What is a vacuous pass?
questions.answer:
a |-> b: check b in the same cycle a holds (overlapping). a |=> b: check b in the next cycle; equals a |-> ##1 b.
Vacuous pass: when the antecedent is false the property passes trivially, so an assertion that never fails may never have been exercised. Pair every important assert with a cover property on its antecedent.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `|->` (overlapping) checks the consequent **in the same cycle** the antecedent matches; `|=>` (non-overlapping) checks it **one cycle later**. `a |=> b` is exactly `a |-> ##1 b`.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",       "wave": "p......" },
  { "name": "a",         "wave": "0100100" },
  { "name": "b",         "wave": "0100010" },
  { "name": "a |-> b",   "wave": "x=xx=xx", "data": ["pass", "FAIL"] },
  { "name": "a |=> b",   "wave": "xx=xx=x", "data": ["FAIL", "pass"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "a at cycles 1 and 4; b at cycles 1 and 5" } }
```

| Cycle | a | b | `a \|-> b` | `a \|=> b` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1 | 1 | pass | starts, checks b at 2 |
| 2 | 0 | 0 | vacuous | **fail** (b = 0) |
| 4 | 1 | 0 | **fail** | starts, checks b at 5 |
| 5 | 0 | 1 | vacuous | pass |

### Vacuous pass
- When the antecedent is false, the implication is **true by definition**. Most cycles of most assertions are vacuous passes.
- Danger: an assertion whose antecedent never happens (wrong signal name, a feature never stimulated, reset never released) passes in every test and proves nothing.
- Fix: pair every important assertion with a **cover** of its antecedent (or the whole scenario), and check the cover count in the regression.

```systemverilog
a_hold: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) valid && !ready |=> valid);
c_hold: cover  property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) valid && !ready);   // proves it was exercised
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `disable iff (!rst_n)` stops evaluation during reset. Without it, assertions fire on X or reset values.
- Many simulators report vacuous successes separately; some count them as passes. Look at the "real" (non-vacuous) success count.

### Follow-ups
- *`a |-> ##[1:3] b`?* b must arrive 1 to 3 cycles after a.
- *`a #-# b` / `a #=# b`?* Followed-by operators: like implication, but they *fail* if the antecedent never matches (used in covers and formal).

questions.title: Write an assertion: valid must stay high, with stable data, until ready (AXI / stream handshake).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** once the source raises `valid`, it can't take it back or change the payload until the handshake (`valid && ready` on a clock edge). So: whenever `valid` is high and `ready` is low, next cycle `valid` must still be high **and** `data` unchanged.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",   "wave": "p........" },
  { "name": "valid", "wave": "01..0.1.0" },
  { "name": "ready", "wave": "0..10..10" },
  { "name": "data",  "wave": "x=..x.==x", "data": ["D0", "D1", "D2"] },
  { "name": "check", "wave": "x.==x..=x", "data": ["ok", "ok", "FAIL"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "D0: held until ready (ok). D1 changes to D2 while ready is low: $stable fails" } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
property p_valid_hold;
  @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  valid && !ready |=> valid && $stable(data);
endproperty
a_valid_hold: assert property (p_valid_hold)
  else `uvm_error("SVA", "valid dropped or data changed before ready")

c_backpressure: cover property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) valid && !ready);
c_long_stall:   cover property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) valid && !ready [*4]);
```

### Explanation
- `|=>` checks the **next** edge: if there was no handshake this edge (`!ready`), the beat is still pending next cycle.
- `$stable(data)` compares the sampled value with the previous edge's value. For AXI, include every payload field (`{addr, len, size, burst, id}`).
- The cover proves backpressure actually happened. Without it, a TB with `ready` always high passes vacuously.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Don't write `valid |-> ##[0:$] ready`: that's a liveness property (ready eventually), which is different and unbounded in simulation.
- `$stable` on X data: X to X counts as stable. Add `valid |-> !$isunknown(data)` as a separate check.
- After reset, `valid` must be low (AXI rule): `$rose(rst_n) |-> !valid`.

### Follow-ups
- *Ready may depend on valid?* Yes, the rule is one-way: the source must not wait for ready, and the sink may wait for valid.
- *Liveness with a bound:* `valid |-> ##[0:100] ready` catches a stuck sink in simulation.

questions.title: Write assertions for a req/ack handshake: ack within 1–3 cycles, req held until ack, and no ack without req.
questions.answer:
p_ack_in_time: $rose(req) |-> ##[1:3] ack. p_req_hold: req && !ack |=> req. p_no_orphan: $rose(ack) |-> req (ack may only rise while req is high).
4-phase handshake: add $fell(req) |-> ##[1:$] $fell(ack) and !req |=> !$rose(ack).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** split the protocol into **one property per rule** (timing, stability, causality) so a failure message tells you exactly which rule broke.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk", "wave": "p.........." },
  { "name": "req", "wave": "01...0....." },
  { "name": "ack", "wave": "0..1.0....." },
  {},
  { "name": "phase", "wave": "x=.=.=....x", "data": ["req up, wait 1-3", "ack: done", "both low (4-phase)"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "req rises, ack follows 2 cycles later, req drops, then ack drops" } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
property p_ack_in_time;  @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  $rose(req) |-> ##[1:3] ack;                  endproperty
property p_req_hold;     @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  req && !ack |=> req;                         endproperty
property p_no_orphan;    @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  $rose(ack) |-> req;                          endproperty  // ack only rises while req is high

a_ack_in_time: assert property (p_ack_in_time) else $error("ack not within 1-3 cycles");
a_req_hold:    assert property (p_req_hold)    else $error("req dropped before ack");
a_no_orphan:   assert property (p_no_orphan)   else $error("ack without req");

// 4-phase (return-to-zero) handshake additions
a_ack_falls:   assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) $fell(req) |-> ##[1:$] $fell(ack));
a_no_new_ack:  assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) !req |=> !$rose(ack));

c_ack_at_3:    cover property (@(posedge clk) $rose(req) ##3 ack);   // slowest legal response
```

| Rule | Property | Typical bug it catches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| timing | `$rose(req) \|-> ##[1:3] ack` | slave too slow / stuck |
| stability | `req && !ack \|=> req` | master gives up early |
| causality | `$rose(ack) \|-> req` | spurious ack |
| return to zero | `$fell(req) \|-> ##[1:$] $fell(ack)` | ack stuck high |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `##[1:$]` is unbounded: in simulation, a missing `$fell(ack)` only shows up as an *incomplete* assertion at the end of the test. Use a bound (`##[1:16]`) if the spec has one.
- `$rose(req)` needs a defined previous value; use `disable iff` so the first cycle after reset doesn't false-trigger.
- If ack can arrive in the same cycle as req, the window is `##[0:3]`.

### Follow-ups
- *Formal:* make the req rules `assume`s and the ack rules `assert`s when verifying the responder.

questions.title: Write APB protocol assertions: PSEL → PENABLE → PREADY.
questions.answer:
Setup phase is followed by the access phase: psel && !penable |=> psel && penable.
While waiting, controls are held stable: psel && penable && !pready |=> penable && $stable({paddr, pwrite, pwdata}).
Transfer ends and PENABLE drops: penable && pready |=> !penable.

questions.title: Write an assertion: B toggles exactly 2 cycles after A toggles.
questions.answer: assert property (@(posedge clk) $changed(a) |-> ##2 $changed(b));
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** "toggles" means the value changed since the last clock: `$changed(x)` (equivalent to `!$stable(x)`). Every change of A must be followed, exactly 2 cycles later, by a change of B.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",        "wave": "p........" },
  { "name": "a",          "wave": "0.1...0.." },
  { "name": "b",          "wave": "0...1...1" },
  { "name": "$changed(a)","wave": "0.10..10." },
  { "name": "check",      "wave": "x...=...=", "data": ["pass", "pass"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "a changes at cycles 2 and 6; b changes at cycles 4 and 8" } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
a_b_follows_a: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
                 $changed(a) |-> ##2 $changed(b));

// stricter: b changes ONLY 2 cycles after a change of a
a_b_only_then: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
                 $changed(b) |-> $past($changed(a), 2));

c_toggle: cover property (@(posedge clk) $changed(a) ##2 $changed(b));
```

| Requirement | Property |
| --- | --- |
| every A toggle causes a B toggle 2 cycles later | `$changed(a) \|-> ##2 $changed(b)` |
| B never toggles on its own | `$changed(b) \|-> $past($changed(a), 2)` |
| both | use both properties |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- After reset, `$changed` compares with the reset-time sampled value; `disable iff` avoids a false trigger on the first cycle.
- If A toggles on consecutive cycles, B must also toggle on consecutive cycles; the properties handle it because each A change starts its own thread.
- "Toggle" for a bus means any bit changed; for a 1-bit signal it's a rise or fall (`$rose(a) || $fell(a)`).

### Follow-ups
- *B toggles 2 to 4 cycles later?* `$changed(a) |-> ##[2:4] $changed(b)`.
- *Equivalent with `$past`?* `$changed(b) == $past($changed(a), 2)` checked every cycle covers both directions at once.

questions.title: Write an assertion: after cat rises, dog is high for 3 or 4 consecutive cycles. Explain the repetition operators.
questions.answer:
assert property (@(posedge clk) $rose(cat) |=> dog[*3:4] ##1 !dog);
[*n] repeats on consecutive cycles; [->n] is goto: the nth occurrence (may be spread out), match ends on that occurrence; [=n] is non-consecutive: like goto but the match may extend past the last occurrence.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `dog[*3:4]` matches a run of 3 or 4 consecutive `dog` cycles. Following it with `##1 !dog` pins the run's **end**, so a run of 5 or more fails.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk", "wave": "p..........." },
  { "name": "cat", "wave": "010......10." },
  { "name": "dog", "wave": "0.1..0...1.." },
  { "name": "result", "wave": "x....=....x.", "data": ["pass (3 dogs)"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "cat rises, then 3 consecutive dogs, then dog low: pass" } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
a_cat_dog: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
             $rose(cat) |=> dog[*3:4] ##1 !dog);
```

### Repetition operators
For a sequence `start ##1 b[…] ##1 end_sig`, with `b` high on the marked cycles:

| Operator | Meaning | `b` pattern `1 1 1` | `b` pattern `1 0 1 0 1 0 0` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `b[*3]` | 3 **consecutive** cycles | match (ends on the 3rd 1) | no match |
| `b[->3]` | goto: 3rd occurrence, gaps allowed, match **ends on** the 3rd 1 | match | match, ends on the 3rd 1 |
| `b[=3]` | non-consecutive: 3 occurrences, match may **extend** past the last one while b stays 0 | match | match, ending on the 3rd 1 or any later 0 cycle |

### Explanation
- In the consequent, `dog[*3:4]` starts one thread per length. The property passes if **any** thread matches: with 4 dogs, the 3-thread fails on `!dog` but the 4-thread passes.
- `[->n]` is common in protocols: `req |-> ack[->1] ##1 done` means "at the first ack, then done next cycle".

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Without `##1 !dog`, `dog[*3:4]` passes as soon as 3 dogs are seen, so 10 dogs would also pass.
- `[*0]` (empty match) in an antecedent can cause surprising vacuous passes. Avoid it unless needed.

### Follow-ups
- *Unbounded run:* `dog[*1:$]` (one or more), or `[+]` shorthand in SV-2009.
- *Cover each length:* `cover property ($rose(cat) ##1 dog[*4] ##1 !dog);`.

questions.title: Write assertions that check a clock period within ±5% and detect glitches shorter than 2.5 ns.
questions.answer:
Use a local variable to capture time at one edge and compare at the next:
p_period: realtime t; @(posedge clk) (1, t = $realtime) |=> ($realtime - t >= 0.95*PERIOD) && ($realtime - t <= 1.05*PERIOD).
p_no_glitch: realtime t; @(posedge sig) (1, t = $realtime) |-> @(negedge sig) ($realtime - t >= 2.5ns).
If PERIOD comes from another domain, sample it into a stable variable, or do the check in a monitor instead of SVA.

questions.title: Write an assertion that an AHB burst must not cross a 1 KB boundary.
questions.answer: assert property (@(posedge hclk) htrans == NONSEQ && hburst == INCR4 |-> (haddr[9:0] + (4 << hsize)) <= 11'd1024);
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** check once, at the **first beat** (`HTRANS == NONSEQ`). The burst's last byte is `start + beats × 2^HSIZE − 1`, and it must stay in the same 1 KB block. With the offset inside the block `haddr[9:0]`: `offset + beats × 2^HSIZE ≤ 1024`.

| HSIZE (bytes) | HBURST | start `haddr` | offset + bytes | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 (4 B) | INCR4 (16 B) | 0x3F0 | 0x3F0 + 0x10 = 0x400 | **ok** (ends exactly at the boundary) |
| 2 (4 B) | INCR4 (16 B) | 0x3F8 | 0x3F8 + 0x10 = 0x408 | **fail** (crosses 0x400) |
| 3 (8 B) | INCR8 (64 B) | 0x7C0 | 0x3C0 + 0x40 = 0x400 | ok |
| 2 (4 B) | INCR16 (64 B) | 0xBD0 | 0x3D0 + 0x40 = 0x410 | **fail** |

```text
1 KB block:  0x000 ........................ 0x3F0 0x3F4 0x3F8 0x3FC | 0x400 0x404
INCR4 @0x3F8:                                         [beat0][beat1] | [beat2][beat3]  <- crosses
```

### Code
```systemverilog
localparam logic [1:0] NONSEQ = 2'b10;
localparam logic [2:0] INCR4 = 3'b011, INCR8 = 3'b101, INCR16 = 3'b111;

function automatic int unsigned beats(logic [2:0] hburst);
  case (hburst)
    INCR4:   return 4;
    INCR8:   return 8;
    INCR16:  return 16;
    default: return 1;          // SINGLE, INCR (undefined length): checked per beat elsewhere
  endcase
endfunction

a_no_1kb_cross: assert property (@(posedge hclk) disable iff (!hresetn)
  htrans == NONSEQ && hready && hburst inside {INCR4, INCR8, INCR16} |->
    (int'(haddr[9:0]) + (beats(hburst) << hsize)) <= 1024)
  else $error("AHB burst crosses a 1 KB boundary at %h", haddr);
```

### Explanation
- `beats << hsize` = beats × 2^HSIZE = total bytes in the burst.
- Cast to `int` so the sum can't wrap at 10 or 11 bits.
- Sample the address phase only when `hready` is high (when the address phase is actually accepted).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- WRAP bursts never cross by construction (they wrap inside their own aligned window), so they don't need this check.
- Undefined-length INCR may legally cross only if the master ends the burst first; check each SEQ beat (`haddr[9:0] != 0` for SEQ beats) if the spec forbids crossing.
- AXI's equivalent rule is 4 KB (`addr[11:0]`).

### Follow-ups
- *Why 1 KB?* It's the minimum address space given to one AHB slave, so a burst can't spill into a different slave.

questions.title: How do you check data through a pipeline with SVA? Which built-in functions do you know? assert vs assume vs cover?
questions.answer:
Carry data with a local variable: (in_vld, v = in_data) |-> ##3 (out_vld && out_data == v + 1).
$rose(start) |-> busy throughout (##[1:10] done): busy high from start until done, done within 10 cycles.
Built-ins: $rose/$fell, $stable/$changed, $past(x,n), $onehot/$onehot0, $isunknown, $countones.
assert: must hold (sim reports failures, formal proves). assume: constrains inputs in formal, checked like an assert in sim. cover: scenario can happen (formal witness, sim hit count).
JasperGold: assumes for input protocol, asserts for outputs; a wrong assume over-constrains and hides bugs — back assumptions with covers.

**Key idea:** a **local variable** captures the input when it enters, and the property checks the matching output N cycles later. Each input starts its own thread with its own copy of the variable, so overlapping transactions are handled automatically.

### Code
```systemverilog
property p_latency3;
  logic [31:0] v;
  @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  (in_vld, v = in_data) |-> ##3 (out_vld && out_data == v + 1);
endproperty
a_latency3: assert property (p_latency3);

// busy is high from the start cycle until done, and done arrives within 10 cycles
a_busy: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
          $rose(start) |-> busy throughout (##[1:10] done));
```

| Function | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `$rose(x)` / `$fell(x)` | x went 0→1 / 1→0 since the last clock |
| `$stable(x)` / `$changed(x)` | x is the same as / different from the last clock |
| `$past(x, n)` | x as sampled n clocks ago |
| `$onehot(x)` / `$onehot0(x)` | exactly one bit set / at most one bit set |
| `$isunknown(x)` | any bit is X or Z |
| `$countones(x)` | number of 1 bits |

| Directive | Simulation | Formal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `assert property` | reports failures | tries to prove it for all legal inputs |
| `assume property` | checked like an assert | **constrains** the inputs (the environment's rules) |
| `cover property` | counts hits | finds a witness trace, or proves it unreachable |

### Explanation
- In **JasperGold** (or any formal tool): write `assume`s for the input protocol the block can rely on, and `assert`s for its outputs. A wrong or too-strong assume over-constrains the inputs and hides real bugs, so back every important assumption with covers showing interesting behavior is still reachable.
- `throughout` requires the left expression on **every** cycle of the right sequence.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Variable latency: use `##[1:$]` with a terminating condition, e.g. `(in_vld, v = in_data) |-> ##[1:20] (out_vld && out_data == v + 1)`. With in-order outputs, a tag or counter is needed to match the right output.
- Local variables can't be used to check *ordering* across threads; use a scoreboard for that.

### Follow-ups
- *`$past` with an enable?* `$past(x, 1, en)` samples only on cycles where `en` was high.
- *`sequence` vs `property`?* Sequences describe patterns over time and can be reused inside properties; properties add implication, `not`, `disable iff`.
